speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member. I do not know whether the Member agrees with the registry of Members' external travels. There is no requirement at this time in the proposed modification to the rules to list trips paid by the Government when the Government sends its own Members abroad, either with a Minister or with some other official delegation.
We feel that would put members of the Opposition in a somewhat difficult situation. We would have to declare our external travels and put forth any expenditures that were incurred at that time and the sources. Members on the Government side, however, would be protected in that if they travel with a Minister or with an official delegation of Government they do not have to reveal these trips. What does the Hon. Member feel about this?

1 think, Mr. Speaker, the Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) has pointed out one of the difficulties in this motion. The McGrath Report itself came up with a

February 13, 1986
Standing Orders
number of recommendations, many of which are supportable and will be supported. However, in the transition from the McGrath Report to the proposed motion a number of Government changes have been injected, one is the notion of the five day naming. A second one is the notion of the registry.
I personally have no problem with any registry. I think Members of Parliament on all sides of the House should be open and above board at all times. I think it creates a somewhat specious view in the minds of the public if on the one hand you have a registry where Members of Parliament, government Members or opposition Members, can travel to Barbados, to Geneva or to Stockholm at the expense of taxpayers and have no public accountability through the registry, while on the other hand you can have Members on a mission or a fact finding tour sponsored by a group, other than the Government, who are fully accountable. I think the accountability should be across the board. That should include a full docket for Ministers as well as for Members of the Government and Opposition for all trips outside the country. It should not be restricted only to the notion of non-government funded trips.
I know from trying to track down Members from time to time that a number of Members are off on trips all over the world. I am not quite sure of the reason because they are with a Minister, it is not necessarily a subject for public discussion.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to respond to one remark the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) made yesterday in a speech to which I listened with care and interest. She claimed that the proposed system by which Government appointments will be reviewed by the committee would be neutered, that there will be no effective authority on the part of the committee and, therefore, it is not a useful reform.
I say briefly for the record that I do not understand the reform in those terms at all. The real effectiveness of the review will come from publicity. The light of public discussion in meetings and through the media will shine upon the appointment, and 1 think that will be a safeguard that any Government will keep in mind when the appointments are put forward.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that there is good reason to believe this is the real effectiveness of the system now employed in the United State Senate. While there is a vote required so that the appointment can be confirmed or denied, the real power of the Senate lies in the publicity given to some nominations, the kind of discussion that is stimulated and which, in the past, has caused some nominations to be withdrawn.
MO)
I do not accept the claim that the committees and the review process have been neutered. I understand the Hon. Member's points but it seems that she has not given sufficient recognition to the effectiveness of the publicity which will arise from committee hearings.

Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member hearkens back to the discussion which occurred in the House yesterday, one of the difficulties I pointed out was that there would be no veto power for the committee. The second difficulty 1 pointed out was that in the proposed motion the Government has a certain prescribed period-I believe it is five days-in which to depose the Order in Council appointments, presumably after Cabinet has made its decision. Subsequent to that there is a maximum 30-day period for examination.
If we look at a period wherein there might be hundreds of appointments, for example, a summer period of two months where we might see 2,000 or at least hundreds of appointments-
Try the day before Christmas.

Or the day before Christmas. The way the current motion is established, we would be allowed to review all those appointments, and the review must be complete within the 30 days following the five days of the deposition. It seems that if we want to do a real thorough analyis and have the kind of public exposure about which the Hon. Member spoke, at the very least there should be no time limit on the period of review. The 30-day period actually hamstrings or handcuffs Members who may in fact want a very throrough review of several hundreds of appointments. In that regard I agree with the Member that some kind of public exposure is in and of itself a good thing.
We see that at the moment there is some public exposure when appointments are made, if they are not made the day before Christmas. However, on balance, if we introduce two elements which include the possibility for a veto of the committee and no time limit for review, we would have a better motion. It would speak to the issue of diffusing power from the Cabinet. Essentially at the moment we are reinforcing the notion that the Cabinet ultimately makes a decision for every Government action. If we are moving toward a reform system, some of that reform will have to entail taking away specific powers which rest now in Cabinet. This is why I think the veto power would be an indication that the Government was prepared to go in that direction.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to make a modest contribution to this important debate on the proposed amendments to the Standing Orders that govern the proceedings in the House of Commons. First of all, I want to say that on this side of the House, at least as far as the Liberal Party of Canada is concerned, we welcome these reforms of the Standing Orders of the House. I believe that the proposals before the House today are part of a number of changes that have been proposed from time to time in the House of Commons, also by the previous Government. In fact, Members who have been sitting in the House as long as I have will recall a major reform that was introduced in 1969.
February 13, 1986

Today, I think we should give credit to all Members on the Special Committee on Parliamentary Reform, chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). Actually, 1 think the recommendations of the Hon. Member for St. John's East and his Committee would probably have been adopted faster than the Government's proposal, and I will get back to this point later on and explain my reason for mentioning it.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, on the subject of parliamentary reform, 1 would like to say a few words about the context in which I feel such reform should take place. The most visible part of that context is the parliamentary system in this country which is based on political parties. In Canada, our political parties represent certain tendencies, certain parts of the political spectrum, which may vary from left to right with all the variations in between. Traditionally, political parties in Canada have over the years represented certain specific political positions with which voters identify. In fact the Canadian electorate fully expects political parties in the House of Commons to live up to their election promises. In other words, let them follow up on their election platform. So people expect the Government to try to implement measures advocated on the hustings. Opposition Members are also expected to scrutinize every Government move and stick to the views they publicly defended, just so they will be true to themselves.
That is why I say that private Members should play a significant role but, as I see it, it is given short shrift because I maintain that political parties have primacy in our parliamentary system. The logical conclusion therefore is that the private Member's role does not weigh much in the balance. Well, not quite! Private Members do play an important role in our system because within their own caucus they help hammer out the policies of their Party and, through their contributions both in the House and in committees, they also do their share to draft and finalize legislation. Still, evidence about the way Canadians choose their Governments-particularly since the early 60s and given the ever growing presence of the electronic media-makes it clear that they cast their votes for political parties rather than for candidates. In my judgment, this factor cannot be ignored in any Parliament reform.
So what are the objectives of the reform? I would simply refer to a very straightforward statement made by the House Leader of my Party, the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), who said: Our object must be to make Parliament do better that which it is intended to do. In my opinion, however, this does not mean that by improving Parliament, we want to make it a machine designed to adopt bills non-stop and full steam ahead. I feel that this would be a mistake. While a number of bills can go through all stages very quickly because they are straightforward or because they are fully supported by all parties in the House, or because their contents are generally felt by the public to be fair, equitable and reasonable, others must be fully and thoroughly considered during a debate which may last quite some time, if necessary.
Standing Orders
This reform of the House should not either make it possible for a limited number of opposition members or even for an opposition party to frustrate the will of the majority. I want to make it perfectly clear, therefore, that I fully support the Government's right to introduce its program as it sees fit, because a majority Government has received a mandate from the people.
What should we aim at? What is needed, in my view, is a balance between the right of the Government to carry out its program and the right of the opposition to bring to the people's attention the fundamental issues and to initiate a meaningful debate on matters and policies that are likely to result in major direction changes. I suggest that this reform should also aim at improving the public's awareness of the House's proceedings, because in a democratic system, the public's input is essential. And since the people are not themselves present inside the House, but are present through their elected representatives, they should be able to see what is going on here. 1 wish television and other media had access to the committees of the House to allow the public to see and editorialize on its own what is going on and not have to rely solely on members of the press gallery who, even though we must admit they do a very good job, act as intermediaries between the public and us, in the House of Commons.
That being said, I would like to state once again that generally speaking we support the Government proposals.
On this side of the House we agree generally with the reform as introduced by the House of Commons. When 1 say "generally", it means, of course, there is a caveat. There are a number of items that we would like to see modified.
The first thing I would like to say from a philosophical point of view is that if this report was a straight translation of the report of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons, chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), it would be easier to pass it through this House because all Members would feel that we were adopting a unanimous report of a committee on which all Parties were sitting. We cannot say that these proposals originate from the committee as they have been modified. The Government has to realize that these are Government proposals.
We do want changes but how are we going to accomplish this? We look at the motion before us and we realize that this motion does not allow amending several of the proposals. How do we go about it? I am happy to see the Government House Leader in the House together with his deputy, and I would like to explore with them how we can achieve that. What my Party would like to see is a change in our rules passing through the House of Commons rather swiftly. Personally I would be happy to go home to my riding for the recess with the pleasure of knowing that we have adopted new rules. If we are to achieve that how do we do it?

February 13, 1986
Standing Orders
I suggest the easiest way would be for discussions to take place between the House Leaders of our three Parties. I gather that discussions are likely to take place soon, and that is probably the best route. Otherwise there is a more cumbersome way that might have to be used, and that is to amend the motion that is before us and refer the proposals back to a committee where obviously specific amendments to some of these specific proposals could be introduced. I say this is too long a process. It would border on the adversarial, and I do not like it. Therefore, I suggest very strongly that discussions take place today while this debate is going on. We should come to some agreement to iron out some of the difficulties-and there are not too many of them, some are menial-so that we may conclude these discussions between Parties with a proposal which would reflect the desire of all Parties. In this way we would follow the tradition over the years of having the rules of the House adopted in a rather unanimous fashion, with few exceptions. We should strive to establish a set of rules with which everyone would agree. It would certainly improve the climate in the House of Commons. This is a goal worthwhile pursuing.
[ Translation]
Therefore, in my opinion, it would be quite worthwhile if the Government met today with the opposition parties and tried to bring in the few changes they are seeking so that we end up with a product that will be acceptable to all. Because it must be recognized that to this day, there have not been any agreement, secret or public, to adopt these changes to the rules without ample debate, which, in my opinion, should result in some adjustments. If we can come to an agreement, I am sure that when we leave at the end of the day, on Friday, we will have new rules, which is what I wish personnally.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to be more specific, I would like to mention some of the changes that have been suggested by some of my colleagues. First of all it becomes clear after listening to those who spoke in the House that many members referred to the problem we are facing regarding the proliferation of legislative committees.
This proliferation is causing tremendous difficulty, especially to opposition parties in view of the unbalance existing in this Parliament between the number of Opposition Members and Government Members. Indeed, by reducing the room to manoeuvre of opposition parties, the proliferation of legislative committees is affecting the quality of legislation, and in the end the public is the loser. In my opinion this is also affecting the climate in the House of Commons whereas the opposition parties with a small number of Members are hardput to believe that they have an important role to play in the development of legislation.
As we have followed the model of British legislative committees, I would suggest that we go a bit further and follow even more closely the British system, under which there are only eight legislative committees and bills must queue up before going before one of these committees. I believe that we should
limit the number of legislative committees, which would certainly allow the opposition parties to do a better job and also stop Government backbenchers from feeling pressured by the great number of bills being referred to committees as no member of this House, whatever his party, can give the required attention to some of the proposals before those committees. This is one thing which should be improved in my opinion and I hope that it will be discussed among the parties.
There is also the registration of trips abroad by Members of Parliament. I think that this is an excellent principle and a very good proposal. However, I am surprised that the proposal involves registration only for the exceptions, that is trips paid by individuals, foreign countries or companies. The major weakness of this proposal is that the most frequent type of trips would not be registered. Trips by Parliamentary delegations would not be registered, whether they are organized by the Secretary for Parliamentary Relations Secretariat or by various organizations, and this even applies, Mr. Speaker, to the delegations that you yourself are sometimes called to lead in other countries, to trips by Ministers or Government representatives, and I am of course speaking about the trips made with the taxpayers' money on official business. These would not be registered either. However, it would be very useful, as we have seen. During the present session. Ministers were already questioned by some members who were not convinced that public money had been spent sparingly enough. Consequently, I suggest that all trips-except the private trips abroad taken by a vacationing Member, which are is private business-relating to the duties of a Member or a Minister be registered. In my opinion, the Registry should be easily accessible. The data should be computerized to allow a quick check by anyone interested as, I believe, foreign travel undertaken by a Member of Parliament in that capacity is a public matter about which any Member of the House, or member of the public or the press should be able to obtain information. Each Member is responsible to his or her voters.
I would also like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, on one of the proposed Standing Orders which would give the Chair important powers to maintain order in the House. Some of my colleagues have already pointed out that giving the Chair the authority to exclude a Member for five days, as proposed under the new rules, was excessive. It seems to me that expulsion of a Member by the Chair, for one day, is quite sufficient. First of all, it prevents the Member from pursuing the objective he or she had in mind when he or she created the disorder. We all know that the following day the argument will have lost much of its impact, especially in these days of electronic medias, and consequently this is enough of a sanction.
Moreover, the publicity surrounding a suspension is bad generally for a Members's image. Indeed, one has to recognize the important principle that there must be some sort of order
February 13, 1986

in the House of Commons, and that the Chair must have the means to enforce it. However, it seems to me that the power to suspend a Member for one day is enough. Going any further would be depriving the Member and his constituents of the basic right to be represented in Parliament.
If I may, Sir, as one who has been a Member for 17 years, I can state that past experience has shown there is no need to give the Chair the authority to suspend a Member for a period of five days. Under the present system, when the Speaker names a Member, it rests with Government to introduce a motion to suspend that Member from the service of the House. But I do not recall any instance during the 17 years I have been here, of the Government introducing a motion to suspend a Member for more than one day. Recently, for instance, the Government could have suspended a Member for three, four, five days, or the whole session, but it never did so. All this is to say that I do not see the need for that, and 1 would be surprised if you yourself, Sir, without putting words in your mouth, would support such a measure.
I would also like to deal briefly with private Members business or bills. In my view, there must be a guarantee that the new system will be tighter than the one that is proposed- that it will not give the Government an opportunity to have important measures accepted as items of private Members' business, because it is a basic principle that the Government must be accountable to the people at all times. It has already been suggested as an example that amendments or a return to the death penality could pass in this House under the guise of a private Member's bill.
This then is all I will say about other changes that seem important to us in those proposals. Besides, other colleagues of mine have already referred to them. I will rather repeat before concluding, Mr. Speaker, that it seems essential to me that this package get the unanimous support of the House so that everyone will be happy, will comply with our Standing Orders and will also respect the Chair who has to enforce them. And it will be easier, Mr. Speaker, to enforce the Standing Orders if the political parties are in agreement when they are passed. As I said, I ask the Government to meet with the Opposition parties or in short to call a meeting of House leaders to discuss some of our problems. I am sure, and I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that if the parties seriously tackle the issue, we will come to an understanding and we could have before tomorrow afternoon a fine set of new Standing Orders acceptable to all and I hope for you, Mr. Speaker, that they will be scrupulously complied with by everyone.

Mr. Speaker, with his experience, I should like to ask the Hon. Member whether he could enlighten us on the problems which have arisen in the committees and how they could be solved or aggravated as a result of the proposed changes.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
There are surely several problems dealing with the operation of committees I do not want to be more specific. But surely the major problem resulting from some of the proposed changes and as experienced during the past few months, is the proliferation of legislative committees which I would say is excessive. As a consequence, a standing committee and a legislative committee may be sitting simultaneously to deal with the same matter. Therefore, a Member who is sitting on both committees has to choose between attending a legislative committee to deal with a bill or attending the standing committee to discuss other matters or some orders of reference received from the House. That is only part of the problem. The other part is the fact that from time to time, and this has actually happened, several legislative committees are sitting simultaneously.
Now this will never be an ideal situation, even when we have a better balance of representation in the House than we have today. But in times when the Opposition is not as well represented as it usually is in the House of Commons, this can be a major problem. Once again, if the Opposition is to make a constructive contribution towards improving the legislation referred to a legislative committee, we cannot let several committees sit simultaneously, and we will have to prevent the proliferation of such committees. I may recall my earlier suggestion, which is that if we want to adopt a model, which happens to be the British model in Westminster, we should adopt it in its entirety, and not just take this concept of a legislative committee and apply it in a way that does not work satisfactorily.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make the following comment and ask my hon. friend, the Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) what he thinks about it.
We know that in the report prepared by the parliamentary committee chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), the recommendation regarding order-in-council appointments suggested that in addition to having a procedure for review of appointments by a parliamentary committee, the committee would also have the right to veto appointments to certain positions.
Mr. Speaker, I think Hon. Members would prefer to have this veto right applied to all positions.
1 also think the Hon. Member for St. John's East wanted to strike some kind of balance, and in his report he and his colleagues elected to set up a system by which certain positions would not only be scrutinized but would also be subject to veto, including positions that are connected directly with the House of Commons: the Clerk, for instance, the Commissioner of Official Languages, and so forth. I think there were about 40 positions that would not only be subject to scrutiny but also to veto.
I would therefore ask the Hon. Member whether he would care to comment on whether we should have this veto right for

February 13, 1986
Standing Orders
all order-in-council appointments, or just for certain positions, as recommended in the report by the Hon. Member for St. John's East, or not at all, as the Government has proposed in the amendments before the House.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, that is one of the shortcomings of the project under consideration. Had the Government chosen to present the special committee report as it was, Opposition Parties would have adopted it without a fuss because we did attend those meetings and agree to the contents of the report.
Unfortunately, I repeat that the Government picked out the provisions it could live with and rejected others it did not like. So we ended up with lopsided proposals, whereas the report presented by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) did strike a fair balance.
With respect to appointments, Hon. Members will not have much more to say under these new provisions. In fact, we do not gain anything. Members will be allowed to call appointees to appear, but in many instances we can do that as it is.
Let us say we want to look into the appointment of a major Crown corporation president. We ask the president to appear before the committee. We can do that now and ask him questions. Under the new provisions, we would do the same thing, but in a different way.
If in some cases the committee had a veto or suspensive power concerning an appointment, as advocated by the Special Committee on Reform of Parliament, then the Government would show it is aware of the fact that it has given or transferred some of its powers to the House, to private Members. But it has not done that.
As it is, it is nothing more than window dressing, a sham, because we already have the power to call as witnesses before the committees the presidents and senior officials of most Crown corporations. This, therefore, does not add much.
What was needed was a legislation with sharper teeth, but the Government dared not, or did not find desirable to act in this direction.
Debate. The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal also with this motion, the purpose of which is to adopt provisional Standing Orders of the House for a trial period of about one year.
Some may wonder why members of the Official Opposition rise in the House one after the other to deal with this motion concerning changes to the House's procedures, when these changes are usually adopted very quickly because of a consensus arrived at between the various parties' House Leaders.
We are rising one after the other to put forward very often the same type of arguments, so that people watching us on TV orGovernment Members could easily conclude that it is repetitive and that the debate is being extended needlessly. But, Mr. Speaker, is that not the very essence of Parliamentary debate? What role could a member or a party play in the House if, whenever there is a difference of opinions, he or she is not allowed to repeat his or her points to the limit and thereby bring about some changes? Indeed, these changes to our procedural rules, even though they are to be provisional, could easily become permanent if the Government chose to proceed, as it is doing now, by using the weight of its majority.
Mr. Speaker, I have not been here that long, but I have had the honour to sit in another Parliament which undertook a complete reform of its parliamentary procedure following what was then called the Lavoie Report, after the representative of Laval who was also Speaker at the Quebec National Assembly. As is the case here with the McGrath Report, we then had the Lavoie Report, which was studied by Members of all the parties and which, in my opinion, had to a great extent met its objective of developing a consensus among the parties on a new parliamentary procedure. To my knowledge, various Parliaments have examined not only the changes that were made, but also the effects that this has had on parliamentary debate.
We are often tempted to compare parliamentary procedure in the House of Commons or in provincial legislatures with the procedures in the American Congress, and to compare the role of a Member of the Canadian House of Commons, the Quebec National Assembly or the Ontario Legislative Assembly to that of a representative in the American Congress. I believe that it is a serious mistake to try to make such a comparison because our Parliamentary systems are completely different and our rules must reflect this difference. It could be said that the major role of Parliament would probably be to debate general policy for public administration.
It could be said that second role of Parliament is certainly to legislate and that its third role is to vote supply and control expenditures.
It could certainly be said that through our debates and parliamentary committees, we try and reach a national consensus on various subjects. I would also say that most of the arguments and much of the disorder take place when Members try to fulfill their role, under our adversarial system which is to make the Government act openly, that is to say to force Ministers to answer for their Department, make them acknowledge in this House and in front of the public the actions they took and explain the reason why they have taken them. Very often, that is were the problems arise, as the Government tries to use its majority to avoid this type of questioning from the Opposition. Under our system, we have opposing teams facing each other. Even the physical set up of
February 13, 1986

this Chamber, Mr. Speaker, is designed that way. It is not quite like that at the present time, because of the results of the September 4th election, but normally you have the Government on your right and the Opposition on your left. The rules and the parliamentary tradition require that the Opposition House Leader, the Government House Leader, the Government Party Leader and the Opposition Party Leader reflect the ideas of their respective caucuses. Consequently, whether we want it or not, we have two machines facing each other. Our whole system revolves around that notion. It is Fine to talk about the role of the private Member, but we have to put it in that perspective. That is why it is not possible, in my opinion, to give a Canadian Member of Parliament the same role and responsabilities given to a representative in the American Congress, because our systems are entirely different. There, Members can propose bills, through their committees, even if they involve expense of public funds. There are all kinds of differences.
Therefore, the rights of the Government and those of the Opposition are set out in parliamentary rules, and in order that each group may adequately fulfil its mandate, we must have fundamental guarantees, and not only for the benefit of today's Opposition. The Conservatives sat on this side for a number of years, and no doubt will come back to it shortly. It is my view that our parliamentary system must protect the fundamental rights not only of individual Members but of the groups within which such Members are working. I have served long enough in political parties to the right of the Chair to know that the Government Member's fundamental role is often played within the caucus. It is so true that it is an important feature of our rules and of our parliamentary system that here, in Ottawa, as in the Legislative Assemblies, contradictions that are publicly aired between Ministers or Government Members or between Opposition Members make the headlines.
I have spent a few days with a delegation of Government Members, Members of all sides of the House who went to Washington to study tax reform. We were privileged to be hosted by the Special Committee which deals with all tax legislation, and so forth. Mr. Speaker, we saw things that do not happen very often in our committees-Democrats and Republicans fighting together against other Democrats and Republicans, who happened to be the Opposition within the committee. Here, the rules are so different that a Government Member who would go to a parliamentary committee and launch an open attack against his or her Minister would no doubt experience the treatment that some Members apparently got recently. He or she would be gagged. And this is normal, because we are teams fighting each other-a Government made up of a majority of Members and dependent on that majority to maintain its position, and an Opposition.
Standing Orders
Now parliamentary rules must reflect that. This is the reason why I submit that in my concept of the British parliamentary system, if we want to change it, I would be ready to discuss it. I do not underestimate the advantages of certain procedures in existence in the United States or in other parliamentary systems. However, as we live under a British parliamentary system, we should be very careful to safeguard the fundamental rights of the Government.
The Government has the right to legislate. The Government has a fundamental right, it has received the support from a majority of voters and thus has a majority of Members. It is entitled to govern.
However the right to govern does not mean that it can stop the Opposition from preventing the passage of some bills. As we see it now. It can be tiresome for a backbencher who would like everybody to be kind and helpful and to ease up the passage of those rules. However, I do not suggest that there are bad things in them, there are many good ones. However, the only tool the Opposition has is this Parliament where the proceedings are held. It would not even be necessary to have so many Members here if the Government made a decision which would have to be approved within half an hour. Surely our Parliament is here for having discussions and as under our parlamentary system some Members are for and some are against, such discussions can only be spirited.
We do not agree on fundamental issues. And the problem is that when we do agree, things go down easily and no one notices. But what catches the eye of the public opinion? Only those issues on which we disagree. That is why people often say to us: The Opposition is wasting the time of the House. But I think it is important to see things in a global perspective.
Consider for instance the matter of old age security pensions which was debated for so long in this place. Can you think for one second, Mr. Speaker, that if we in the Official Opposition had just been content with two or three questions and, seeing that the Government was not amenable to our point of view, and we had said: Well, there is nothing else we can do, we have no right to come back for three or four days in a row on the same question and to annoy all Government backbenchers, can you think for one second that the elderly people in Canada would now have fully indexed old age security pension? Do you think that in the case of family allowance, for instance, even if we did not succeed eventually, in spite of a previous commitment by the Government, do you think that we in the Opposition had no right to belabor that matter regularly?
I could mention a number of other instances, and 1 will therefore, before I conclude, mention also some of the suggestions that were put forward. And there again, Mr. Speaker, I will not mention those issues on which we have agreed, but rather those which warrant a careful approach.

This happened with the legislative committees and that experience was referred to by my colleagues. Especially when the Opposition, as is now the case, is made up of only 40 Honourable Members; however it does not mean that the institutional role of the Opposition should not be fulfilled. As a matter of fact, when we had so many legislative committees, my colleague of Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) literally had to run from one committee sitting to another, sharing has time between the Standing Committee studying matters related to immigration and two other legislative committees which were considering bills dealing with issues coming under her scope of activity. Finally, one has only 24 hours in a day to eat, rest a little and mostly, as a member, do research work. After a week of that strenuous regime, a Member is faced with the problem of finding time to read and do research in order to properly discharge his on her duty.
That is why we believe that this proliferation of legislative committees is not in the Parliament best interests and that their number should be limited or at least, that a more restrictive use should be made of them.
1 am also concerned with the matter of maitaining a registry of trips taken by Members of Parliament. I agree that there should be a registry and I think it is a very good idea; 1 would even say that it is essential, and I know that my colleague from Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) has often raised this question with me, even before I came here as it was one of his pet projects. So, maintaining a registry is certainly a good idea.
But why maintain a registry of a very restricted number of trips by Members? If I am a member of a delegation of the Association internationale des parlementaires de langue fran-Qaise, to which I belong, and leave with the delegation for a francophone country of Africa, say, I do not see why my name should not appear on the registry for anyone to see, including the media. The same thing could be said about a Government Member who would accompany a Minister travelling to the Francophone Summit, why should that not be recorded in the registry? I think the only exception would be trips made by a Member at his own expenses, whether he is on holidays or decides to travel to study something at his own expenses. That would be the only exception, everything else should appear on the registry.
Another matter which I find rather intriguing and which should be of some concern to you, Mr. Speaker, is the authority which the Chair would have to suspend a Member for five sitting days, without any kind of motion. This brings me back to what I said a moment ago: there is a reason why this institution is called the House of Commons. You know, that name just did not happen to drop from the sky, it could have been called the House of Lords, the House of Academics, or even the House of Canadian VIPs. No, Sir, it is known as the House of Commons because we represent the people and all classes in our society, and debates can be nothing but lively. I often come across some of my friends who have nothing to do
with politics, they watch television and say: My God, what a lively place, you cannot even agree with one another! Well, if we all agreed, we would not need Parliament. Just look at municipal councils with five, six or ten aldermen. Their meetings can go on until midnight or one o'clock in the morning. Obviously, as soon as a bunch of people meet in the same room to discuss a matter, they may or may not agree, and if they do not, they will have to argue their points according to certain rules of parliamentary procedure, and that is why we need those rules to protect the rights of Members.
In the course of parliamentary debate, in which there may be considerable animosity ... For instance yesterday, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) did not, we felt, give a clear answer to a question he was asked about unemployment insurance. He gave the impression that the rules had not been changed and that the matter had been referred to the Forget Commission, while letters had been received, and of course all members received the same representations, complaining that people were not receiving unemployment insurance benefits if they were drawing a pension. In a case like that, the debate tends to get heated. We cannot just go along with the fact that the Minister rises in the House and knowingly or unknowingly fails to reflect a situation that was quite obvious. Mr. Speaker, it is quite understandable that in a case like that, Opposition Members are furious, and that is what we are here for. Our role is to act agressively enough to make the Minister reconsider and give us the information, and also to make sure the general public is informed.
If in the course of debate, Members happen to raise their voices or if on the spur of the moment, because a Member is absolutely convinced that he is right, he uses words that are unparliamentary, Mr. Speaker, you will call him to order, and you may do so once or twice, but to give the Chair the authority to expel a Member from the House for five days . . . If I were in the Chair, that is one prerogative I would not want to have, because it is a dangerous one, and I am thinking of what might happen in a major debate. When Maurice Richard was benched for five consecutive games before the Stanley Cup play-offs, it caused a riot at the Montreal Forum. Imagine, in a crucial debate, imagine the pipeline debate, if the Leader of the Opposition, John Diefenbaker, had been expelled for five days, imagine what the reaction would have been in the House!
So this is one prerogrative which I consider excessive, and I feel we ought to find a way to changing this particular Standing Order, and if we could do this outside the House, in Caucus, and with representatives of the various parties, 1 think it would be in the best interests of all concerned.

Given the good knowledge that the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) has not only of the federal but also the provincial political scene, I would like
February 13, 1986

to ask him to clarify his views on the matter of the five-day suspension. I think that other Hon. Members might want to speak about it. When he mentioned that the Opposition Leader was really involved in the pipeline debate, will the revised Standing Orders, the proposals that are now before us, in effect cut off debate or not?

Mr. Speaker, the incumbents change but the office remains. What I wanted to emphasize when I made a comparison with the pipeline debate ... In fact, to everyone who followed politics in the late 50's-my colleague from Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) is too young to have been around when this debate took place, but it was towards the end of my academic studies-that debate was a turning point in Canadian politics and even probably brought about the change in Government in 1957 and 1958. That debate was really lively and hot and I wanted to underline that the new Standing Orders would give the Chair such huge powers that I cannot see how a Speaker could apply them while maintaining order and decorum in the House. That would undermine the nonpartisan role of the Chair because it could easily be argued that the Speaker suspended a Member of Parliament for five days under the pressure of the parliamentary majority which is in power. Even today, under normal circumstances, a Member is expelled for one day on the House's initiative and not the Speaker's. I think it is very significant that in our parliamentary system, the Speaker or the person who is in the chair in the House of Commons or any other Legislature at the provincial level, is the humble servant of all Members of Parliament. He does not act as a judge who gives rulings but he is the servant of all Hon. Members. This has been reflected traditionally in all kinds of rules and interpretations. Therefore, when a Member is suspended, it is by the House itself by means of a vote.
I know that the procedure has been made easier in other jurisdictions. However, this custom results from the fact that since the Speaker is the servant of all Hon. Members, he cannot both take action persona proprio motu, as both judge and jury. He may designate a member by his name and it is the House itself that will expel him for a day by upholding his decision. I find it excessive to give the Speaker such a power ... If the objective is to save time, we might replace this by a vote to be taken immediately, within ten minutes. At the present time, the vote must be taken within the next thirty minutes, which I find excessive as I said. However, as concerns the question you raised, I think that the principle that must prevail in our rules is that the Chair is not a judge but the servant of all Hon. Members and that it should not be put in such a situation that it could be easily accused of bias.

Mr. Speaker, I want to go back to the other question raised by my hon. colleague for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) and the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). It concerns the committees in which all members are involved. The Hon. Member might share his experience
Standing Orders
with us as I think he is a member of several financial committees which seem to be non-partisan and one of which is chaired by an Opposition member.
Could he tell us if the multiplication of committees will be a good thing or if it will be too difficult to find a sufficient number of members within the Opposition's ranks.

Mr. Speaker, I find the question asked by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) quite interesting. First, why did we appoint Standing Committees, and not only here but in other legislatures? Because we wanted some questions to be examined in depth by groups of Hon. Members; after a while they become in a way experts in agricultural matters or in international affairs. If you have been for a long time a member of the Committee on Agriculture, even if you are not familiar with the farm community and agricultural problems at the beginning, after two or three years, you become fairly well briefed on the subject. Standing Committees are composed of Hon. Members who chose in the first place to become members and who said so to their House Leader, who agreed. Secondly, they have not only an interest in the subject because they chose that committee, but they develop expertise.
If we appoint more and more legislative committees, it means that at a certain time-it was the case with the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs-it becomes impossible for three or four persons to cover the whole area. The Hon. Members who become experts in Standing Committees become useless when Bills dealing with a particular subject must be examined because it becomes impossible to cover the whole area, in particular in a situation like this one, where every Hon. Member, in particular Opposition Members, both on the Liberal and on the NDP sides, must be a member of two or three committees.
If this is a means this majority Government is using in order to have its bills adopted quickly, it should come right out and say so. But if such is not the case, and if it is sincerely seeking new mechanisms for individual members to get more directly involved in the consideration of the many bills, there should be a procedure, as suggested earlier by my hon. friend from Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault), to determine which legislative committee will sit, where and at what time, and set up a work schedule which will make it possible for these people to carry out their duties both as members of the House and members of the committees.

I should like to ask him next-about the committee issue. On the basis of his experience sitting on the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, does he feel that committee members are more efficient when they address a general problem with a great many ramifications, or when they concentrate on only one or two subjects? For instance, when it dealt with the failure of the Commercial Bank of Canada, the committee spent a lot of time studying

the problem thoroughly. On the other hand, other committees are exposed to such dissipation that members who are supposed to attend do not because nothing concrete ever comes out of their proceedings. That is why there were problems during the trial period.
Would the Hon. Member agree that if we were to accept the proposal as it has been implemented during the trial period this year with the new committee system, it would be a good idea to be able to review the whole process before the end of the 10-month period, as suggested in the motion?

Mr. Speaker, if we take for example the committee which considered the failure of the Canadian Commercial Bank and Northland Bank, this Committee had to examine those issues just about at the same time as it was considering the Green Paper on the Reform of Financial Institutions.
Only to give an example, while the date when this committee would meet had not been chosen at the time, if the Committee had also had to examine Bill C-84 and C-80, which dealt with financial matters, it would have been complete chaos. It would have been completely impossible, not only to make an in-depth study to see where the Government had made mistakes in the bank failures, since the Government had to bear its share of responsibility in this affair and it was our duty to say so to the Canadian people, but we would also have been unable to make an in-depth study of the amending legislation, for instance to deindex personal income tax tables and provide for substantial tax increases. The committee could not have reviewed such legislation at the same time.
I am not saying that this is the intention of the Government at this time, but it would certainly become extremely tempting for a parliamentary majority to use this mechanism to prevent the Opposition from doing its job. This could provoke a strange backlash if the majority were to impose by force these new rules instead of doing so by consensus. It could come back to haunt them and they might be the first to critize the rules when they change sides three years from now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask another question on another matter, namely petitions and Order Paper questions. Certain changes have been proposed of which the effect would be to cut off a Member asking his fourth question or presenting a petition with only 22 or 23 signatures. I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) whether he agrees with me that, if a few people in his constituency want to present a petition about a problem which exists either in their riding or in Canada as a whole, they should be entitled to do so in the House of Commons without any restrictions being imposed because there are not as many of them as big companies, for instance.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Debate. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak briefly on the reform of the House and I do so in all humility being a new Member who was elected at the last election. I cannot pride myself on having the expertise gained with years of experience by some of my colleagues on both sides of the House. However, I had the opportunity in the past to sit in another legislature, namely the Ontario Legislature, where for a few years I had the privilege of representing my constituents in that House so that I can compare at least two different forums and try, if you would allow me, to tell you about the good points which relate to both Houses and indicate where the present system needs to be improved.

The first thing I want to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, is the structure of legislative committees as we now know them. Under the last reform of the House of Commons, the House adopted a system which provided for new committees. This looked extremely good on paper, of course, because we could then strike a committee of people who had a particular interest in the topic or in the piece of legislation. That committee, with its expertise and knowledge, could deal with a Bill about which it knew something.
One would ask what could be wrong with that. Well, nothing is wrong with the structure. However, unfortunately, whether or not it was inadvertent, the system was abused. At this time some Members of the House are members of so many committees that it would be physically impossible to attend all of their meetings even if they were awake 24 hours a day and never left the Parliament Buildings.

I will give you an example, Mr. Speaker.
I for one am a member of the Standing Committee on Agriculture. This Committee does plenty of work for people in my constituency and a great many other areas in Canada- that work is very important as we know. I also sit on the Committee on Public Accounts, which reviews Government expenditures. I also have been appointed to many other committees, and I will tell you about some of them. I sit on the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, which has a very
February 13, 1986

important role as you would say. I sit also on the Committee on Procedure and Organization, the Legislative Committee on Bill C-45, the Committee on Bill C-87, the Committee on Bill C-256, the Committee on National Resources and Public Works. Thus, as you may see, Mr. Speaker, I sit on seven or eight different committees of this House.
Besides, as every other Member does, 1 have constituents- there are 100,000 of them in my constituency-with all the problems faced by constituents everywhere. Since 1 represent a rural constituency, we all know this entails a lot of travelling around, and I see some Members opposite agree to that, because they are in the same situation. We must also sit in this House to represent our constituents in this, the highest court in the land. Also as Members of Parliament, we have to meet in caucus with members of our own political parties. In that respect, I chair the Ontario Liberal Caucus. So this entails rather frequent meetings.
I also sit on this party's caucus' executive, which meets twice daily to plan questions or issues which must be raised in this House, and so forth.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think you realize that something that was well intended has in fact become a parliamentary monster, and it is absolutely impossible for a Member to do his work under the circumstances. The number of those committees must therefore be reduced at all costs, and it must be ensured that those who have been elected, even in a minority party in this House, can go on performing their duties not withstanding.

I want to raise with you the issue of Order in Council appointments. The committee chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) published a report of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons. I believe that by and large that was an extremely good report. I want to congratulate the Member for St. John's East and the other members of the committee who worked so diligently to prepare that reform package. However, I resent the fact that the Government chose to adopt only those portions of it which it saw as advantageous to it and neglected to adopt those portions which were perhaps less favourable to the Government of the day.
The governing Party should remember that, although it is presently sitting on the Government benches, that situation is not permanent. On occasion Parties change positions in the House, as they did in the last election, and as they will again. If I may be partisan, I hope that will happen sooner than later. While trying to keep my tone rather non partisan, I do say that the governing Party should remember that these rules are made for the House as a whole rather than for the Government. The rules should be designed to enhance the role of Members regardless of which side they sit on.
The Government adopted only certain portions of the report, and one of the portions it omitted has to do with Order in Council appointments. Under the provisions of the report of
Standing Orders
the Member for St. John's East, nominations by Order in Council would be reviewed by a parliamentary committee. That is what the Government wants to do at the moment. However, the committee recommended that there be a right of veto over certain political nominations, certain nominations by Order in Council. An example of this would be the officers of this House; the Clerk of the House, the Auditor General, the Commissioner of Official Languages and a certain number of others.
I think it is important to note that in order for those people who are charged with the functions I have just described to function properly, they and many others should have the support of all political Parties and, really, all Members of this House. What better way is there to ensure that those appointees enjoy that confidence than by giving a committee of Members of this House a right of veto over those appointments. Unfortunately, the Government did not see it that way. It chose to give a right of examination, which is good, but certainly not as effective as giving a right of veto.
I would like to speak briefly on the travel registry, Mr. Speaker. I am sure all Members would probably wonder why, if I do not, having been the personal subject of a minor amount of controversy on the topic.
Last fall, Members will recall, I had the opportunity, having been asked by a fellow Member of the House of Commons from another political Party, to join a parliamentary delegation visiting Taiwan. The delegation was composed of Members on both sides of the House; seven Conservatives, two Liberals and one with no political affiliation.
I did some research, asking whether the trip was precedent setting. In other words, was it the kind of trip that usually happened. I learned that Members of Parliament had been to Taiwan on six or seven different earlier occasions. I inquired whether the trip was partisan or non partisan.
There were people from both sides of the House involved, and that sounded all right. I wanted to know whether the trip was to be paid by another country, non-profit group or the Government of Canada. I learned that the trip was to be paid by a non-profit organization in the host country. That sounded all right as well. Finally, I asked who had gone on previous trips, only to discover that approximately a dozen present Members of Cabinet had been on the same type of trip to Taiwan.
Along with the other Members, I went. It was a very interesting trip. I informed my electors of the trip before I left through a press release. Some would say that was probably the mistake I made, but I had nothing to hide.
As things turned out, Mr. Speaker, some controversy arose over the trip; not in my view because I had gone, but perhaps because I had criticized others in the past who had partaken in certain ventures that caused large expenses to the Government of Canada with little or no benefit.

Pursuant to that particular episode, the Government decided to study the possibility of having a travel registry. The purpose of this registry was to ensure that everyone knew where Members were going and who paid for the trips.
I draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that a Cabinet Minister could, right now, fly to Europe every third or fourth day all year round on an Armed Forces plane and never register that fact under this proposed registry. In other words, a Member of Parliament or a Cabinet Minister could take 75 trips a year to Europe and not have to register them. On the other hand, a Member who takes a trip, such as the one I took last year, would.
There is nothing wrong with any Member having to register the trips they take. Why is it that a Cabinet Minister or a government member or others can travel with a member of Cabinet on a government jet or on an Armed Forces plane outside the country and not have to account for it to anyone, while an opposition backbencher has to account for every move he or she makes?
I will not be so cynical as to claim this whole process is an attempt by the Government to stop members of the Opposition from doing anything so that they can themselves partake in those activities to a greater extent because they, being on the government side, have very little if any accounting to do for that kind of activity.
If the Government wants to have any kind of fairness at all, it is very important, and I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you will recognize this, that all trips taken for all reasons outside Canada by any elected person in this House be accounted for.
As I indicated in the past, I have nothing to hide. I never attempted to do so. That is the way it should be for every Member of the House of Commons. Let us register where we are going every time we leave the country and who is paying- if it is not ourselves on a personal holiday-whether the Government of Canada, a Government of another country or a group. Everyone should be able to view the document and to question whether a Member of Parliament has been to Europe nine times in 13 months, or if a Member has not gone any place in the last four years. There may be very worthwhile reasons that a Member had to go to Europe that frequently, but he or she should be able to account for it. Some correction is needed in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the new Standing Orders regarding the suspension of a Member from the service of the House. I am speaking as a Member who may on occasion have come close to being asked to withdraw from the House, although this has never happened yet in the course of my political career, neither at the provincial level nor here in the House, and I hope it never will. And I say this with my usual sincerity, the same sincerity I apply to getting my views across in the House and making the Government account for
its actions, but I certainly hope I will never see the day that I am suspended from the House by order of the Speaker.
And I can understand, let us say I could tolerate a situation where the Speaker could have a Member removed from the House or suspended from the House for one day. In fact, that is what happens in the Ontario Legislative Assembly.
However, I prefer our system where the Members themselves decide whether a Member should leave the House. 1 think this enhances the role of the Speaker, reminding us that he is the servant of the House, not its master. I am sure that you, Mr. Speaker, will agree.
But to recommend that the Speaker have the authority to suspend a Member for five days ... I am sure that you, Mr. Speaker, being the reasonable person you are, would not want such authority. To have such power is a dangerous thing! It is dangerous because, I believe this would mean the Speaker would no longer be the servant of the House, as I said before, but its master. I am sure that is a role that neither you, sir, nor your successors in the Chair would wish to have. I just wanted to raise this point, Mr. Speaker, which is in fact the most contentious aspect of the amendments before the House today. I would urge the House leaders of all three parties to meet before the end of this debate and withdraw this particular section from the proposed amendments. I feel it is totally inadmissible, being the most contentious of all the recommendations made for parliamentary reform. It is a symbolic gesture, Mr. Speaker, but it is important to each and everyone of us.
The constituents in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell elected me to represent them in the House and not outside the House for five days, and especially not by order of another Member, even if that Member happens to be the Speaker. Should the electors of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell ever decide they want a Member thrown out of the House they can always resort to the electoral process, as can others in all constituencies in Canada, and they have been known to do just that.
I insist on this point, Mr. Speaker, because it is very important, and I would urge Government Members to express their views about this since it is a non-partisan aspect of the proposed changes to the Standing Orders. 1 think we are now dealing with the most significant proposal and, with all the conviction I can muster, Mr. Speaker, I must say I do not agree that anyone-except our electors-should enjoy the privilege of throwing a Member out of the House, especially not for five sitting days.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) about the point he has just raised at the end of his remarks, namely that under the new Standing Orders the Speaker would be allowed to name a Member and suspend him from the proceedings of the House, first for one day and then, as a result of
February 13, 1986

successive incidents which would prompt the Chair to name him a second time, for five sitting days.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member and the House know very well that the suspension of a Member is the object of a procedure whereby the Speaker names the Members. Second, normally in support of the Speaker, the Government must move a motion. The motion calls for a division and it is only after the vote that the Member involved is suspended and must leave the House. As far as I know there is nothing in our present Standing Orders which would prevent the Government from introducing a motion pursuant to which any Member might be expelled or suspended from the House for one, two, three, five days, a week or more. Nothing in the Standing Orders provides that the Member must be suspended for the rest of the sitting day. I stand to be corrected, but in my brief experience here in the House I have never heard anything about a Government moving a motion to suspend a Member for more than the rest of the sitting day. Nowhere in my research did I find one instance where a motion was introduced to suspend a Member for more than one day.
That is why I would suggest the Hon. Member is quite right to say that it would be giving a lot of authority to the Speaker, the kind of authority which perhaps the Chair itself would not want to have. 1 would like to support him and I will have the opportunity to deal with this issue in a speech this afternoon. I agree with the statement he has made to the effect that the Government could try at least to reduce this power which I feel is excessive and give the House the authority to ask an Hon. Member to withdraw from the House.
I would like to direct a question to the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, if I may. He said that his constituents were the only ones who could deprive him of his right to speak out in the House, and I agree with him that he could be deprived of this right following an election, but I am sure- and I would like him to confirm this-that he has enough democratic sense to realize that if he has caused a disturbance which his peers feel is serious enough to warrant a warning or an exclusion, his peers in the House, his own colleagues, could move a motion to express their condemnation of his behaviour or conduct in the House, or could they not?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) is quite right in that obviously a member who creates a disturbance makes it impossible for the House to operate, and in so doing, is abusing the privileges of all the other members of the House. A member who behaves like this prevents the constituents of all the other Members from being represented. Which means that all other Members together have the power, the privilege and indeed the duty to expel this member in order for their constituents to be represented in the House. I will even go as far as to say that it is not only the privilege of other members to propose such a motion, but also that it is their duty to suspend an unruly member. However, as was mentioned by the Member of Ottawa-Vanier, as far the
Standing Orders
government has never suspended a member for more than a day, namely the day of his misconduct. Why then does the Government want to give this privilege to the Speaker when we know that it would never use it itself? Would the Government like to give the Speaker a responsibility which it would not assume when it could have done so? That, Mr. Speaker, is the crux of the matter. The Government, even with its current majority, or any previous Government with a different majority, has always been reluctant to use this power and throw out a Member for more than a day, the day in fact when his conduct in the House was unruly. Why is that so? There are several reasons for it. First of all, Government Members themselves recognize that the suspended member's constituents have the right to be represented in this House. Therefore his suspension should only last until order is restored, after which the debate should resume, Mr. Speaker.
As you can see Mr. Speaker, even a Government with a very large majority is reluctant to use a power it wants to give to someone else. Does it mean that they are trying to force the Speaker to do something that they did not have not the courage, or did not deem necessary to do? I ask this question in all sincerity. The answer is probably no; it is probably not what the Government wishes to do. I will even give it credit by saying that it is not the case.
If it is not the case, Mr. Speaker, why do not they take this opportunity to withdraw this part immediately, because obviously this is a mistake which the Government House Leader has made. These things happen Mr. Speaker, when only half of the recommendations of a Parliamentary Committee report are accepted with subsequent deletions and additions. Had the Government decided to introduce the McGrath Report in its entirety, all this controversy would not have taken place today. When additions are made at the last minute, a problem such as the one the Government must now face with regard to that portion of the project, can arise.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Exactly!

Naturally, it is because these additions have been made at the last minute without prior consideration in Committee. So it is a mistake, and I am even willing to admit that it is a mistake on the part of the Government. I think that part of the proposal should be withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, I have two questions for the Hon. Member of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). One is related to the Order Paper Questions. Would he know if as a result of these changes, fewer than four questions can be addressed to the Government at the same time? I would like to ask him whether he agrees with this initiative. If not, why?
If you allow me, Mr. Speaker, I will now ask my second question. It relates to the registry, a recommendation which has been added to those of the McGrath Committee report,
