speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order! The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), on a point of order.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish simply to rectify a comment I made earlier when I said that inasmuch as I knew, the House had never suspended a Member for more than a day. Somebody immediately called me to say that I was wrong. That is why I want to quote citation 25, in Beauchesne's Fifth edition of Parliamentary Rules and Forms, about calling a Member by name. It says:
(5) The penalty common in Canada is suspension for the remainder of the sitting day. On one occasion the House decided upon a seven day suspension-
Mr. Speaker, I think that that was in 1944. It happened only once in our history, but I wanted to tell the House so that Members would not be misled by my earlier statement.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to clarify what I said yesterday in commenting the speech of the Hon. Member for
St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) from Newfoundland, who is also chairman of the committee.
First, I would like to congratulate the members of this committee, especially its chairman, the Hon. Member for St. John's East, as well as the co-chairmen, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), and the other members, they presented to the House of Commons a report in both official languages entitled: "Report of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons". They worked with patience and integrity and they did a great job.
I must say that the recommendations made to the House were of course not all implemented or endrosed by the Government, which then presented, as it was entitled to do, not only the comments on the report which are now required by the Standing Orders, but also this proposal which we have been asked to approve.
Many things strike me, Mr. Speaker, and as I said yesterday, there are some points which should be clarified in the French and English versions as concerns the first point on which I would like to say a few words, namely the expulsion of Members from the House by the Speaker.
First, I must say that for a Member to be expelled is the ultimate punishment. I have always said and continue to believe that the Speaker of the House and his representatives, such as yourself, have an ultimate power against Members of Parliament in case of total disorder. However, since this is an ultimate weapon, they must show a lot of discretion in using this power and do so only after showing a maximum of patience, after reminding a Member on whatever side of the House of his duties as a parliamentarian, and after having appealed to him because, in fact, the Speaker is not the master of the House of Commons, but its humble servant whom we have chosen and whom we shall soon elect ourselves to lead the debates. He is therefore not the master of this House, but he is the one who, humbly, after being chosen by his peers, has to maintain order in the House. However, he does so at the request of the Members. One of us is asked to become Speaker and to ensure that there is order in the House. And if this indeed becomes impossible, he will be given the ultimate weapon of asking that a Member be expelled. Until now, this ultimate weapon of the Speaker is subject to a motion introduced by the Government and calling for a vote because it is so radical a punishment that the Member in question has to be judged by his peers following a ruling by the Speaker, who must, with patience, and even with paternalism or maternalism as the case may be, appeal one, two or three times to the Member in question. He must even if possible humiliate him before his peers and say: I know that the Hon. Member is an intelligent man or women, and I know that the Hon. member would want me to do my duty, which is to maintain decorum in the House. I know that the Hon. Member will understand the difficult situation in which I find myself, but I have to
February 13, 1986

name him a first time. If the Member insists, the Chair, which always has the supreme stick of suspension must have the patience to dialogue with the Member, to calm him down, to ease the atmosphere of the House rather than inflame it. But if the Member will not hear reason, the Speaker then says. "I name you for a second time". And the third time, it is the supreme stick falls down, suspension from the service of the House.
Therefore, it is so final that personally I believe that such a punishment must remain within the hands of Members. The Government has deemed fit to ask us to transfer to the Chair the use of that ultimate punishment, to give it authority to name a Member for a first time, to exclude him for one day.
And where, in the English version, a Member would relaxes, well it is provided that-
The Standing Orders indicate that on a subsequent occasion in the same session the Member shall be suspended from the service of the House for a period of not more than five sitting days.
[ Translation]
Well, I think this is clear in English.

In English it is very clear. However, the first part refers to the Member being once named. What does the word "once" mean? Does it mean the first time, the second time, the third time? My interpretation of the word "once" could mean all of that. It should be made clear that this applies to a specific Member once named for the first time, etc., etc.
As far as I am concerned, there can be a few misinterpretations in the English text. It is not as clear as I would like it to be. I believe English is a precise language, but in French the rule is very clear. Why do we not use the French translation of the English text and put it back into English? If we do, it will not read the same as it does now because the first part of the French text says "Pour la premiere fois"-for the first time. In English the text should read "for the first time".

It is so elementary-

It is clear to me.
Where the rule is not clear in the French version is in the second part of it. In English, the second part of the rule refers to a subsequent occasion, and I would imagine that that is clear unless I am corrected by some of the scholars who are here. There are a great many here who are proficient in the other official language, the one I am speaking. If I am wrong, it is because that is the way I learned English.
By the way, I learned to speak English in the House of Commons. It did not cost Canada a penny. When I arrived here, I did not understand a word of English; I speak English.
Standing Orders
I learned it here without any schooling. It did not cost the taxpayers a penny.
Hear, hear!

I do not say that for the applause. For some Hon. Members, I have to agonize as the Chairman of the Members' Services Committee for the language training school.
If I may say so, one of the best ways to learn the other language is by listening to it in the House. Now I am speaking English. If Hon. Members would like to practise, they could listen in French and It would almost be like an immersion course. Gradually they will be able to catch some of the language. As well, when speeches are boring-and I hope that mine is not-Hon. Members could follow English text line by line with French text. The same thing could be done while attending legislative committee meetings. Hon. Members would learn new phrases and new terminologies that way. In any event, I am not here as a teacher but I do mean to do a little humble duty.
Before this is disposed of, I would like the language of the Orders to be clearly understood. I would like to give a chance to those Members who would like to switch channels now-
[ Translation]
In French ... in French-
The French version says: "le depute qui est designe par son nom une deuxieme fois". And what does happen, Mr. Speaker, the third time? We have on idea, because that is not clear. It is so clear in French "pour la premiere fois", it is not clear if we want to suspend him several times. And one of the risks, Mr. Speaker, after having pondered over that last night, because I was asked to speak on that, but this afternoon rather than this morning, when it is said:

-during the course of a session-

"During the course of a session." There should be a definition of what a session is. You know very well-

I am certainly not going to preach and say that the Liberal Government was better. A session has never been defined. In the past, sessions could last two and a half years, three years or three and a half years, if my memory serves me well, and my Whip will correct me if I am wrong.
For many years, I felt as I am sure most new Members do that a session was to last a year and that there would be four sessions per Parliament. However, bad practices were introduced by past Governments, and I imagine even by some of my own Liberal Governments. In the past, sessions lasted far too long. That now means that there is a danger for an Hon. Member who is more fiery than I may be and less ready to listen to all calls to be reasonable. Such a Member might be frightened to participate in debate in the House of Commons

February 13, 1986
Standing Orders
because if he is suspended a first time, how vigorous may he be later on in a very difficult debate?
I may remind my esteemed new colleagues of an unbealiev-able event that took place here one night during the constitutional debate. Many Members who were then on this side of the House went up to the Chair and, while the Chair was reading the motion, shook their fists at the Chair. As well, during the pipeline debate the mace that is a symbol of authority was almost broken. Those Members were not named by the Chair and the ones who stormed the Chair were right where the pages are, or even closer, with their hands up against the then Speaker, our now happy Ambassador to Portugal, not the proposed Ambassador to Portugal.
We have to be very careful with two things. First, we have to be careful with what we mean in both French and English because the translations are not the same. Second, we have to define what is meant by a session. We have to be precise about that, otherwise there might ultimately be a dangerous tool in the hands of the Speaker. We want the Speaker to have that tool so that he is able to deal with an unruly House and expel a Member once for a day and another time for five days. I am not clear about the language there and I would like it to be made much clearer.
I turn now to the days we sit. As of last Monday, I have been in the House for 22 years. 1 have an old pet project. I believe that the time has come for us not to be frightened, as some Members are, of public opinion. We should explain to the public what it means to be a Member of Parliament in Ottawa. Later on, I will deal with the question of explanations of trips abroad, but right now I will concentrate on what a Member of Parliament is.
A Member of Parliament is someone who works in a Parliament which sits 10 months a year, more or less, for five days a week. In Quebec, for instance, and I am not blaming our provincial counterparts, the Legislature sits for three days a week and perhaps three or four months a year. The same is true of other legislatures. However, we sit five days per week. But, if we are to be good Members of Parliament, we must look after our ridings. I can tell new Hon. Members that if they look after their ridings they will have a hell of a good chance to come back here, but if they neglect their ridings and be too attentive to Ottawa, they will have less of a chance to return.
A good Member of Parliament who is attentive to his duties has to go to his riding on the weekend. Because of this, I have always thought that the House should not sit on Friday afternoons. I lost again because that has not been proposed here. I am not in favour of cutting off debate and providing less time for Government business. I can remember being here every Friday afternoon for 22 years, because I enjoy what I call the Friday-afternoon club. There are very few of us who are here. We get to know each other better. In fact, Mr. Stanley Knowles was always here to represent his Party but he was always alone. He gave a holiday to everyone else and told them that he would hold down the fort on Friday afternoons.
We know that duty calls in Ottawa, but at the same time we would like to be in our ridings. I believe it is nonsense to have the House sit until five o'clock on Friday afternoons. We should adjourn much earlier. The hours that we may lose could be picked up on Friday morning by sitting from 10 o'clock until two o'clock with no lunch hour and the one hour of Private Members' Business we lose could be picked up on Tuesday evening by providing two Private Members's Hours rather than one on that day.
I think the time has come for Hon. Members to start a petition asking that the House adjourn early on Fridays. I am ready to start up a petition along with all of my colleagues from the Government side and the NDP who believe that this proposal makes sense. After all, if we cannot keep our own house orderly, we do not deserve-

subtopic: THE PHILIPPINES-REPORTS OF FRAUD DURING ELECTIONS
THE PHILIPPINES-REPORTS OF FRAUD DURING ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to voice growing Canadian concern about the outcome of the Philippines elections.
Reports from four independent sources continue to state that massive vote fraud is favouring one side over another. Since Canada had an observer present who has prepared a report, I would like to urge the Government to forward this report to the Government of the United States as a reflection of our concern that democratic processes be scrupulously followed.
The Philippines are a significant trading partner of Canada. They are an emerging nation on the Pacific Rim which will have important relations with Canada in the years ahead. A substantial number of people who have come from the Philippines are now living in Canada.
We wish to see the Philippines taking their place as a political democracy with the institutions and democratic processes which mark democratic nations. The Philippines cannot attain this status while staging show elections and remaining a client state of the United States. Canada, as a former colony, knows what is needed. We should take an abiding interest in assisting other nations to shed their colonial status and emerge as fully-fledged democratic nations.
I trust the Government of Canada will effectively transmit this message to Manila and to Washington.

subtopic: NECESSITY OF MAINTAINING FULL ACTIVITY AT DORVAL
NECESSITY OF MAINTAINING FULL ACTIVITY AT DORVAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in recent weeks, the press has been referring to a report that is
to be submitted this March to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). The report is said to recommend a reduction in activity at Dorval Airport, short of closing the airport altogether.
If this recommendation is correct, it defies all logic and would certainly be disastrous for the entire Montreal area. The airport provides direct services to a population of four million and work for 14,000 employees. It is a focal point for the economy of Montreal and of Quebec as a whole. It is estimated that over 100,000 jobs are dependent on the airport, either directly or indirectly.
Transferring domestic flights to Mirabel is not a solution, Mr. Speaker. Not only would services deteriorate because of the greater distance from downtown, but Montreal might well lose its leading position in the aeronautics industry. Furthermore, some carriers might take advantage of this opportunity to concentrate their operations in Toronto instead of moving to Mirabel.
If all flights with connecting flights departing from Mirabel were routed to Mirabel in the first place, under-utilization of Mirabel would be less acute and people would stop talking about taking away from Dorval the air traffic for which it was created in the first place.
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking on behalf of the mayors of Montreal's West Island who are demanding that operations at Dorval International Airport be fully maintained.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR STRENGHTENING LAW AGAINST DEPICTION OF PORNOGRAPHIC VIOLENCE
SUPPORT FOR STRENGHTENING LAW AGAINST DEPICTION OF PORNOGRAPHIC VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cros-bie), as well as the members of the Fraser Committee, on their proposal to amend those Sections of the Criminal Code that deal with pornography. Most Canadians agree that pornography is dehumanizing. It degrades both the men and women that it depicts. Of particular concern, however, is the brutally violent pornography which is becoming increasingly prevalent in our society. I refer particularly to that material which depicts the sexual abuse of women, and even more despicably, of children.
The present laws dealing with this type of material are subjective and ambiguous, making their enforcement very arbitrary and ineffective. The proposal of a three-tier system, while it may not be fully satisfactory to everyone, is certainly a step in the right direction.
Although many people are still disappointed that any pornography would continue to be available even to adults, the majority of concerned Canadians are relieved that the produc-

February 13, 1986
tion or possession of pornography involving children or depicting violence against women will soon be punishable by up to 10 years in prison.
Pornography serves to perpetuate unacceptable myths about women, and if Canadian women are to attain the equality which they deserve, these sterotypes must be destroyed. This proposal is a good start toward that goal.

maintopic: NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT STUDY OF ASBESTOS
NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT STUDY OF ASBESTOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again asbestos is on trial as a result of the United States Environment Protection Agency's latest recommendations that asbestos be totally banned from that country within the next ten years.
It seems to me that such a decision is grossly exaggerated because it has been clearly and scientifically established that asbestos can be used in total security.
I come from one of the major asbestos-producing region and I can formally certify that the people who work in asbestos mines and depend on them for their livelihood are just as physically and mentally fit as the residents of any other Canadian community.
Asbestos substitutes are not the solution because the potential impact of their components is unknown.
On the plus side, asbestos has been analyzed, tested and tried in every imaginable way over the past decades. It has been acknowledged throughout the world that most often its properties are irreplaceable and a boon to the security of users in various sectors.
The logic of the opponents of asbestos is quite questionable and very discriminatory indeed, for the unavoidable conclusion would be that the ban be extended to cover a number of products which are just as hazardous and even more dangerous and harmful than asbestos when they are improperly used.

subtopic: CHANGES PARLIAMENTARY REFORM WILL BRING TO HOUSE OF COMMONS
CHANGES PARLIAMENTARY REFORM WILL BRING TO HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Today, Mr. Speaker, I should like to help Canadians realize how different Parliamentary life will be following the implementation of the provisional Standing Orders of the House.
Mr. Speaker, we have just set in motion the Parliamentary reform process, and gradually over the next few days, there will be a change of attitude and a greater involvement on the part of Canadian men and women in future legislation.
Part of this change will result form the fact that individual members will no longer be compelled to vote along party lines, except in the case of non-confidence motions.
This will translate into an enhanced participation and an increased responsibility for individual members of the House. There will be also a change of attitude among Canadians. They will get involved more, they will express their opinions on the various bills, and try to influence us one way or the other.
Such will be the change of attitude.
Our contribution will be enhanced and our responsibilities increased.
Mr. Speaker, I believe elected members will be more representative of their communities. They will better express the views of their constituents and vote according to their conscience.

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to announce one of the key initiatives of the Government's agenda for economic renewal.
Today I am introducing the first statement of regulatory policy ever articulated by a federal Government and the first strategy for implementing meaningful regulatory reform on a national basis.
Regulation is the chief instrument used by Parliament and by Government to constrain private behaviour and limit freedom in the common interest. Obviously, it is difficult to think of regulation as anything but good if it advances an aspect of
the common interest-for example, controlling the safety of baby cribs, the quality of the environment and the regulation of monopolies.
Can it ever be bad? The insight of regulatory reform says that even regulation that seems otherwise good can sometimes balance out against the public interest.
Regulation begins to go against the public interest when it overwhelms personal freedom, undermines personal responsibility, penalizes hard work or stifles the creativity of conscientious Canadians.
Our awareness that there had been years of indiscriminate regulatory activity led this Government, in the fall of 1984, to identify regulatory reform as a key element of our agenda for economic renewal.
In this context, the Task Force on Program Review last year conducted the most comprehensive and intensive regulatory review ever undertaken at one time in any jurisdiction in Canada. Its work on regulatory programs was complemented by a separate study of policies affecting federal regulatory agencies carried out under a special mandate given to me in September, 1984, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). This work has been integrated into the over-all regulatory approach I am announcing today.
As you know, Sir, the hard word of the program review was carried out by study teams made up of individuals drawn more or less equally from the private and public sectors. The private sector volunteers represented the professions, big, medium and small business, labour and consumer interests. Their mandate was to make federal programs simpler, more understandable and more accessible to the public. The emphasis of their work was on better service to the public, less red tape and greater efficiency. They were not simply concerned with cost cutting. They did an outstanding job, and on behalf of the Government of Canada, I express deep appreciation for their dedicated service.
Let me now turn to the findings of the regulatory review. The study team's diagnosis was certainly none too comforting. The scope of federal regulation is mind-boggling. There are 146 full-scale regulatory or regulatory-related programs and that figure does not even include the Criminal Code. The programs are administered by 35,000 public servants at a cost in this fiscal year of $2.9 billion. In the latest consolidated version, which is already out of date, the regulations fill over
10,000	pages in 19 volumes and weigh nearly 40 kilograms or, for comparison's sake, close to the weight of a 100 pound sack of flour. New federal regulations or amendments to existing regulations have been churning out at a rate of more than 100 per month. The preceding Government lost control of the regulatory system; their best estimates of its scope were understated by half. We found that there was no planning mechanism for regulatory activity and no effective system for controlling its growth. Getting these problems under control will be an important part of our new regulatory reform strategy.
February 13, 1986

At nearly $3 billion, the direct cost to the Treasury of federal regulatory activity is bad enough. However, it pales in significance compared to the cost to the economy of federal regulation; that is, the price paid by individual citizens, companies, non-profit organizations and so on as a result of regulation-imposed costs. The program review estimated the cost of federal regulation to Canada's economy to be at least $30 billion per year, a dimension which has been missing from decision making on new regulatory proposals until now.
Sir, the figures I have quoted refer only to federal regulation alone. The study team found that the scope and cost of regulatory activity by provinces and municipalities is at least as high. So as individual Canadian citizens, we not only pay taxes to three levels of Government, we pay a huge indirect regulatory price to at least three layers of regulators as well.
The major conclusions of the study team were as follows.
First, the cumulative effect of regulation at the three levels of Government constitutes an enormous impediment to economic growth, initiative, enterprise and personal freedom in Canada.
Second, federally elected representatives do not have adequate control over regulation and the regulatory system.
Right on.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Third, the public has too little access to and involvement in the development and review of regulation. Now, that is quite an indictment and we intend to do something about it.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The regulatory review did not prescribe wholesale deregulation as the desirable solution to the problems it found, however, it did identify a large number of existing regulatory programs needing reform in the sense of substantial improvement. With the benefit of the regulatory review's diagnosis and recommendations, the Government has decided to implement a comprehensive regulatory reform strategy. That strategy will have several elements. Indeed, the program review should itself be seen as the first element in the over-all strategy. Today I am pleased to announce two additional elements of that strategy: The adoption of the "first-ever" federal regulatory policy, and, on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), I am now announcing the appointment of a Minister responsible for regulatory affairs.

The fundamental objective of the Government's policy is to promote economic renewal and job creation by improving the management of regulations established by the Government, eliminating those that impede growth and encouraging the private initiative and the independence of businesses through an improved regulation framework.

The policy consists of 10 guiding principles.
Statements by Ministers
First, a reformed approach to regulation is and will remain a necessary and important instrument for achieving the Government's social and economic objectives. However, the Government intends to "regulate smarter".
Second, the Government recognizes the vital role of an efficient marketplace and a dynamic entrepreneurial spirit and that regulation should not impede those values without the most persuasive justification.
Third, the Government intends to limit as much as possible the over-all rate of growth and proliferation of new regulation while protecting the public wherever appropriate.
Fourth, priority is to be placed on reform, but there will be no program of wholesale deregulation.
Fifth, the Government will ensure that regulatory benefits clearly exceed costs before proceeding with new regulatory proposals.
Sixth, regulation will be brought more fully under the control of elected representatives.
Seventh, the Government will increase public access to and participation in the regulatory process.
Eighth, the federal regulatory system will be streamlined and made more efficient.
Ninth, the Government will place priority on increased regulatory co-operation with the provinces.
Tenth, a Minister for regulatory affairs will be appointed while individual Ministers with regulatory mandates will exercise their responsibilities in conformity with the spirit and objectives of this policy.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that anyone familiar with regulation will recognize the significance of these ten broad policy principles. For the average citizen they boil down to the Government's intention to stem the growth of regulation, especially economic regulation, and wherever possible to get the existing regulatory burden off the backs of productive Canadians.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The policy makes clear our intention to tilt our regulatory emphasis in the direction of economic efficiency, market flexibility, and personal freedom. Yet it also confirms our intention to protect the public through the use of regulation wherever it is the best and most economical instrument for doing so. This Government knows that Canadians know best how to run their own lives. They want a Government to support their efforts, not to direct them.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are eager to reform all those regulations which second-guess business judgment or stifle initiative. In that respect, the policy is particularly oriented to small and medium-sized business which is the main creator of new jobs in our economy.

February 13, 1986
Statements by Ministers
The new Minister for regulatory affairs will be responsible for over-all implementation of the regulatory policy and regulatory reform strategy. The Prime Minister has asked me to inform the House today that that Minister is the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn), our most estimable House Leader.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Members will know that the President of the Privy Council is also Chairman of the Special Committee of Council which has the job of reviewing and approving regulatory initiatives. The special committee itself will be given increased authority and responsibility for regulatory matters under the new policy.
The Minister responsible for regulatory affairs and the Special Committee of Council will be supported by a distinct regulatory affairs secretariat to be located in the Privy Council Office with a net saving of person years by virtue of the closing of the two offices heretofore responsible for regulatory expertise; namely, the Office of Regulatory Reform and the Technical Advisory Group, both of which were located in the Treasury Board.
Today my purpose has been to launch our new regulatory reform strategy and to underline the importance which the Government attaches to meaningful regulatory improvement. There are several additional and quite distinct dimensions to the over-all concept of regulatory reform which will be made clear over the next few months. These include special provisions for public participation and access, a package of regulatory improvements, system reforms, a federal-provincial initiative, and important reforms affecting regulatory agencies. Taken together, the various elements of the Government's regulatory reform strategy will comprise the most comprehensive and coherent regulatory reform initiative ever undertaken by one administration in any jurisdiction in Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It will place Canada's federal regulatory policy and practice in the forefront of western countries. Most important of all, Sir, the regulatory reform strategy provides a further demonstration of this Government's commitment to economic renewal through more efficient, more open, more accountable, and less intrusive Government.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to match the excellent performance of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) en frangais by making some of my remarks in the language of Shakespeare.
First, I would like to thank the Deputy Prime Minister for providing us with a copy of his statement well in advance. This has not been customary for all Ministers on the other side of the House. This is a very good example which should be adhered to by other members of the Cabinet when they have statements to make in the House.
This being said, I would like to thank the Government for letting us know that it intends to do something about regulation in the country. This document says just that. It says the Government intends to do something, but it does not say much about when or how it will do it. In fact, without being too vicious, I have rarely seen so many words-12 full pages of them-that say so little on the specific direction and methods the Government will take to solve the problems that have been outlined. Some directions are shown, but little is said about how the objectives are going to be attained and when.
On the first page of his statement the Minister gives us the impression that this is the first time the Government of Canada is doing something about the proliferation of regulation. The Hon. Member for Simcoe-North (Mr. Lewis) is nodding in apparent agreement with this statement. Memories are short. I am certain that if the Deputy Prime Minister and other members of the Government looked back they would remember that regulatory reform was started under the Liberal Government awhile ago, not only with rhetoric but with specific measures. For example, perhaps they will remember the Office of Regulatory Reform which was put in place by a previous Government. That organization had the mandate to publish regulatory agendas of Departments showing plans as to when regulation was to come about and inviting public input. Perhaps the Government has taken some inspiration from these past moves. There is one thing which we would like to know which is not in this statement. I understand that this program has been stopped. If I am right, as I think I am, I would like to know why that is.
Finally, I would like to go into some specifics. Let us look at the 10 guiding principles on pages 8 and 9. This is where the meat, if any, is found. I do not want to go through all of the items, I just want to indicate how some of them are vague. The first item simply says that the Government intends to "regulate smarter". What else does the public expect from the Government? However, if the Government intends to become smarter, that may be welcomed by the public.
The second big guiding principle is that the Government recognizes the vital role of the marketplace and wishes that regulation should not impede those values without justification. We all agree with this. I would say that this is sort of a motherhood statement. The same applies to number five: "The Government will ensure that regulatory benefits will cearly exceed costs-". We would not expect the Government to say the contrary.
Let us move to number six where, I believe, we find an important point. It says: "Regulations will be brought more fully under the control of elected representatives". This is definitely welcomed. It is needed and would be an improvement, but why is the Government saying that at the specific time it is doing exactly the contrary? For the past few days, and even today in the House, we have seen Members attacking the Government, especially the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), because regulations regarding unemployment insurance have been changed, something that affects people in the country. The Deputy Prime Minister
February 13, 1986

knows that. He has written his colleague a letter. Members of Parliament were not consulted. As a matter of fact, backbench members of the Government are angry at their own Ministers for having proceeded in such a fashion.
I hope the Government will state not only that it wants elected representatives to have more control over regulations but that it will end up doing that instead of the contrary. If the ordinary back-bench Member of Parliament is to have some input in regulation, may I suggest, as an improvement, that instead of having one committee of the House looking after regulations arising from legislation maybe the Members of Parliament who have passed a certain Bill in a certain committee should be the ones to look after the regulations that follow a certain Bill. It makes sense to me. Maybe the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) would like to look into this suggestion.
Another item of these guidelines says that the federal regulatory system will be streamlined and made more efficient. I am all for this. I believe it is again some sort of motherhood statement, but let us be wary and make sure that streamlining regulations will not again bring us tainted tuna, buffalo meat that is not proper for consumption, veal that has been injected with steroids or wine adulterated by antifreeze or other products. It is very important that regulations be stringent enough so Canadians are protected. I am sure the Government would like to bear this in mind when looking at the way regulations are made.
Finally, there will be the appointment of a Minister for regulatory affairs. This may be a good thing. I am not sure. It will depend upon the relationship between the Minister and other members of the Cabinet. I presume the new Minister will be co-ordinating the efforts of other Ministers. Obviously each Minister will have to have some responsibilities with regard to regulations arising from Bills that his Department brings forward in the House. It may be good, it may not. The whole scheme may be good.
I am going to put an old saying on the record. The proof of the pudding will be in the eating. Let us wait and see. [Translation]
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I will sum up my remarks by saying that we have before us a document which expresses good intentions in the area of regulations, a document which remains somewhat vague all the same. As I said, it is a shower of words in a vacuum of ideas. There is not much specifics in there. We have to go through a dozen pages before finding three or four points which give a certain direction to what the Government intends to do.
As a matter of fact, this document can be summed up this way: The Government has apparently decided to act in the area of regulations, and the general thrust seems to that be of reducing their quantity.
It does not say how or when the Government will act.
Statements by Ministers
The Deputy Prime Minister's statement in fact seems to be saying: We will seek to do what is right and avoid what is wrong. Yet, it does not provide much infomation on the way the Government will achieve this.
Perhaps the Government could have thought this thing over before coming to the House, in order to give us better indications on what it is really planning to do.
Nevertheless, this is a first step, and I want to congratulate the Deputy Prime Minister for bringing to the House this important document.

Mr. Speaker, I read the statement provided in advance by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen). I want to thank him first for having done that. It is a practice the Government has been following that is a very useful practice in the preparation of some reasonable responses.
I want to begin by saying that, in a sense, this reform, like many reforms, is acceptable. The idea of reform itself is a good idea. I think the Government in bringing forward the reforms is, in many ways, in step with the public's desire to see things being changed that have been in place for a very long time. There is no question that there are a large number of regulations. The Deputy Prime Minister makes that point in his report, and he is absolutely right.
Over the years we, in this Party, have advocated such things as tax reforms and reform of labour standards. We have advocated and supported reform of Parliament. We will in a very general way certainly be interested in participating in the reform which the Deputy Prime Minister has indicated he intends to have the new Minister for regulations or some similar name undertake.
It is a positive step if Members of Parliament are involved in the process all the way through. There is no question about it that regulations have a way of growing on their own without any checks and balances, and the necessity to review those regulations and to determine the effectiveness, appropriateness, usefulness or necessity for the regulations is a process that we in this Party would subscribe to.
Having said that, I want to discuss for a moment or two the whole question of regulation, and put to the Government some concerns that we have about possible courses of action which might be taken that would not be desirable.
It is not always easy to identify the more positive aspects of something. The Deputy Prime Minister I am sure would agree that it is easier to identify the possible negative effects. 1 want to highlight those in order that we do not run afoul of them during the process of review of regulation and deregulating, as the Government has indicated it will do.
Let me read from a document that we prepared in response to the freedom to move document. It is an extract from what the Canadian Labour Congress put in its brief in that regard dealing with regulation. It reads:

February 13, 1986
Statements by Ministers
Government regulation is an attempt to state certain minimum social standards of behaviour that apply to any activity in our society. These minimum standards are a reflection of the social nature of economic activity, the role of Governments and taxpayers and workers in making that activity possible and the minimum rights that accrue to them as a result. Regulation, then, is not a "cost" that can be measured against a hypothetical unfettered market situation, but an assertion of general social rights that are as legitimate as the right to engage in business or the right to earn a profit.
1 say that because it must surely be against that kind of a backdrop that the Government undertakes its review and undertakes its new approach. Clearly we cannot see regulations simply as a cost to be borne. We have to look at them in terms of the benefits one derives, that society derives, from certain kinds of regulations. Although it may be that certain regulations do in fact impose a tax, that tax being a cost, or that certain other regulations do inhibit freedom of choice, by their very nature they are necessary to protect the public from inappropriate actions that can and, sometimes have in the past, been taken by others who do not have but themselves in mind when they make their decisions.
Many of the regulations were brought about as a result of actions in the market-place or in other parts of society that were deemed totally inappropriate by society as a whole.
Pollution.

As my colleague says, pollution regulations for example. For many, many years we were unable to identify the sources of much of the illness that is created in certain parts of the country. It only came laterally to the minds of many that these illnesses were the result of pollution that had been unrestricted. Therefore, regulation of one kind or another has to be put in place. We must keep that in mind as we look at the whole question of regulation, what it is intended to do, where it came from in the first place and what caused it to be put there. We cannot rely solely on the goodwill of others to ensure that safety standards and protections will automatically be maintained if regulations are eliminated or abolished. That will be the way that this Party will approach the question of the review of the many regulations which are in place. In fact, I would venture the opinion that, although the Minister says that there are countless volumes of them, we have to look carefully to try to understand what caused the regulation to be put there in the first place and then make sure that there is in place some alternative means of protecting the public from an unacceptable action taken either against them or by someone inadvertently which causes them harm.
There is potential danger to Canadians in a wholesale program of deregulation. We have seen evidence of that in other parts of the world. We have to guard constantly against the tendency of Governments on the right to believe that somehow or other getting the Government off the backs of people, which is the phrase most frequently used, frees those people to do things they would be desirous of doing without any detrimental effect to themselves or to anyone else.
For example, the deregulation of banks by its very nature causes people to have concerns about whether or not banks are
safe, stable and using good and sound practices. That is not necessarily a particularly desirable thing for Government to do. If the deregulation of trucking, as it inevitably does, means that we will be able to send something more cheaply from point "a" to point "b", there will not be any guarantees of the safety standards necessary to guarantee that if we happen to be on the same highway we will not be the unwilling victims of accidents caused by a lack of proper maintenance. We must weigh that, and I come to the conclusion, therefore, that the deregulation of trucking, if it takes place in any wholesale way, has to be measured carefully against the potential for danger.
There is no doubt that one will be able to take a cheaper flight from here to some other point if the airlines are deregulated. However, will the airplanes be as safe? Will the necessary maintenance have been done? Will the checks and balances still be in place to guarantee that when we are up there we will get down safely? I think the record shows that there are some serious safety questions emerging in the United States now as a result of the deregulation of the airlines.
Over the course of the last few days we have been dealing in the House with a very serious accident. The Government has indicated, through the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski), that it intends to move toward deregulation of the railroads. But at what cost? It is becoming increasingly more apparent that the safety standards and inspection procedures are questionable even now. I predict that the deregulation and the necessity for cutthroat competition, which will supposedly result in lower costs, will result in a very dangerous situation. There is the potential for a very dangerous situation when it comes to safety and maintenance of the rolling stock and rail beds.
What good does it do to be able to buy a cheaper can of tuna if in fact it is cheaper as a result of not having been properly inspected? Of course that would flow from deregulation within that particular industry. While I accept the need to look at regulations very carefully and the proposal for reform of the regulations and the regulatory system, I caution the Minister that reform must always take second place to safety, that reform must always take second place to consumer protection, and that reform must always take second place to the paramount importance of guaranteeing that the public of Canada will be protected from abuses which flow from a market system that makes it very difficult to maintain a proper level of safety and maintenance. What becomes at risk, particularly in certain consumer areas when one starts to attack regulations, is the reputation built up over many years and acknowledged by the world of the quality of Canadian produce which we sell. As we are looking at the potential for deregulation, we must always bear in mind that there are other costs far greater than the cost of maintaining, updating and publishing the regulations which protect us from abuse.
I do not envy the Minister his role, not for one moment. It will be a very difficult task. To the extent that the Government is sensitive about the matters I have raised-and I have only touched the tip of it-there may well be room to reduce the amount of regulation which is currently within our society. I
February 13, 1986

will be the first to applaud when we uncover the areas where it can be done without social costs. However, I suggest that the Minister bear in mind that the free market system, the one which he and his colleagues are so eager to promote, carries with it certain dangers that can and have in the past resulted in inferior product and inferior work. With that in mind, the cost to Canada of deregulation in certain areas and the cost to individual Canadians of deregulation in certain areas, therefore, could turn out to be far greater than the cost of maintaining the regulation now in place which has been identified by the Deputy Prime Minister in his statement.

speechtext:

What happens if the Member in question already has four questions on the Order Paper? Will his oral question have to wait or has the Hon. Member already considered it might be possible to maintain the present formula, which has not been abused by Members, and also that one should not limit the number of written questions on the Order Paper of the House of Commons?

Mr. Speaker, I am starting to regret the fact I did not put in my name for the McGrath Committee, because then I would have had a chance to elaborate on all these questions.
It is true that as far as the vote is concerned, my Whip and I do not see eye to eye.
The Party Whip would like to go on as is, and I think we should have electronic votes with the exception of votes on matters of great importance, on which all Members should have the opportunity to rise and be counted. I will not say which issues are of great importance. Each of us has our own issues which we feel are of great importance including the death penalty, abortion, the Budget and votes on non-confidence. Yes, I believe there should be electronic voting but with exceptions. Therefore, I am not totally in agreement with my very competent and tough Whip who does a good job. [Translation]
As to trips by parliamentarians, I think the time has come to stop all this hypocrisy. For years I have wanted to do this, because people see it as a big mystery, and Mr. Speaker, 1 really do want to answer that particular question, because it affects all parliamentarians, and I am sure that I will have the
February 13, 1986

unanimous consent of the House for saying what my experience has been in the last twenty years.
We are federal Members-

We are federal legislators. If I were not interested in international affairs, I would have run provincially. As a Member of the House at the federal level, I believe that it is my duty to be interested in international affairs. I am sure we would be able to explain that to the people who question these trips taken by Members. I am not afraid to explain that to members of the press if they give us a fair trial and I am not afraid to explain it to the people if we are given a direct connection, as we have now on television, with the people.
It is important that federal Members get to know the world and it is important that they introduce Canada to other parts of the world. I am not talking about Europe but more especially about the non-allied countries. When a Parliamentarian meets a counterpart in the eastern part of the world, he knows that that counterpart is directly connected to power. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, that is my experience. When we meet parliamentarians in all the international bodies, usually they are directly connected to the Head of State or to those who run their countries. These issues are not as sophisticated as all that. And the contacts parliamentarians can make can only benefit Canada, and they can also be useful in showing others how we operate in this country.
We are being asked everywhere: How do your parliamentary committees operate? What does such a thing mean? What does that mean, officers of the table? Those people have not experienced the same development as we have in Canada which is a very fortunate country. Therefore we should not be afraid to go on those trips. And then on our return to the House, we should be given the opportunity to use 20 minutes of House time to report.

That is what there is in the Senate. Every parliamentary group which travels abroad has the flexibility to report back. In this way people can read what went on while it was away. Accordingly, I think the time has come to cut off the secrecy with respect to parliamentary trips. We are grown up men and women; we can take our responsibilities seriously. We can explain. If we cannot, and if we chicken out, then all we have to do is not to accept a trip abroad. If there is some mystery involved, then one does not have to go.
I believe that a book should be kept somewhere, perhaps in the Speaker's Chamber or even with the Clerk of the House, in which Members would write: "I, so-and-so, was the guest of such-and-such government", or: "I, so-and-so, went to such-and-such as a member of a delegation". I do not think this record book should be kept just for certain trips. For example, this Friday I am going to represent my Party at the Francophone summit.
Standing Orders

With respect to the Francophonie Summit, I have been asked to represent my party. There will be 1 NDP member, 8 PC members and four ministers. I do not see why that should be registered in a book even if it is an official delegation. Then all the members are treated on the same footing.

On the question of trips, it is a well known fact that every time a Minister goes abroad he or she brings along what I used to call the favourite Member. Nobody knows of this until several months after the trip when a colleague will say to the Minister: "I heard you went to such-and-such with so-and-so". Why should that fall under this veil of mystery, as if something not quite kosher had taken place? I appreciate the openness. 1 think that is what we should defend. Canadians want openness. I believe the men and women of the press will know what openness means. They will also know that everyone is being treated equally.
My colleague asked me questions with respect to electronic voting and trips taken by parliamentarians. As far as questions on the Order Paper are concerned, I agree with the Hon. Member. I have not made up my mind so I will leave the matter to the House Leaders who, at the moment, are deliberating on the matter.
I conclude by saying that the time has come for us to deal with these matters. Last night I spoke with God and she told me that she would prefer Members of Parliament to pray in public. What is so mysterious about the prayers of parliamentarians? I think we should have open doors and an open confessional which will truly represent the multicultural aspects of our country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with some hesitation because of the eloquence and inspiration which has been provided by the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme). It is always a pleasure to listen to a Member, who has such great experience and longevity in the House of Commons, give us the full benefit of his wisdom. I mean that with all sincerity. It is unfortunate that the rules of this place allow only a 20-minute presentation. We could have spent much more time listening to someone who has such a great wealth of ideas and views expound upon how we can improve our working place and how we can make it a better and more effective arena for the representation which we are all here to perform.
I offer my more limited credentials in this debate. The other night while I was picking up some papers from my home town, where I was reporting on the recently called election, it dawned on me that it has been some 13 years since I first found myself in an elected assembly. While that may not be long by comparison to the time which my friend, the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Isabelle), has spent here, the fact of the matter is that 13 years does give one a certain sense of both the privileges which one has in being a member of an elected chamber and the strangeness of life which ensues once elected. As we all know there can be no greater honour than

February 13, 1986
Standing Orders
having a group of one's fellow citizens choose one to come to this place full of grand hopes and expectations about what we can achieve, only to find oneself convoluted and convulsed by all the strange and exotic mysteries of how to make it all work.
After 13 years one thing which has impressed me greatly is how, over the years of evolution of parliamentary procedure, a remarkable balancing act has taken place. What we do not recognize is that Parliament is really a whole series of dichotomies, a whole series of opposites. There is the Government versus the Opposition, which is the standard type of see-saw we see. There are many others. There is the executive branch versus the legislative branch. One tries to make decisions while the other tries to hold the decision accountable. Obviously, there is an important balance between the interests of the individual Member of Parliament and those of his or her caucus. These factors also have to be balanced out. Every day that we show up for business in this place there is a balancing act taking place. There is an attempt at trying to find some type of harmony of symmetry with the issues of the day. There is an attempt at trying to find some way of making it all work so that things do not get out of balance. That is why a debate with respect to the rules is so important. The rules can substantially shift where the priority, the emphasis, the weight, the power and the influence lie in Parliament. If one makes a wrong choice with respect to the rules, if one shades them too far in one way, then one gives distinct advantage to one of the particular balancing acts about which I spoke. We know, for example, that if a football league decides to change the rules which apply to wide receivers and it prevents the defence from bumping them as they come off the scrimmage line, then one immediately gives advantage to the offence. Similarly, one can change the rules and all of a sudden the defence will have an extreme advantage.
The questions we have to ask are: Where do these rules come down? How do they affect the balance in terms of the workings of Parliament? How do they affect the rights of individual Members versus those of the collegiality to which they belong? How do they affect the balance between the Government and the Opposition? How do they affect the balance between the executive branch which makes decisions and the legislative branch which holds them accountable?
Certainly, the stated purpose of these rule changes as articulated by the special committee and the Government House Leader in presenting them to the House is to give greater emphasis to the individual Member of Parliament. Of course, that strikes music to the ears of individual Members, which is why 1 think that in many cases there is a natural inclination to support these particular proposals. We must also ask ourselves to what degree they may shade or push even further out of balance some of the other legitimate and important functions of this place. The role of Parliament is not just to have individual Members arrive here to present their own particular case. Obviously, the most important function is to hold accountable the actions of the Government. That is what makes us so distinctly different from any other form of Government.
The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that he wishes he had the same rights as the President of the United States and that he would not have to show up for Question Period every day. I suppose anyone who serves as a Minister would share those feelings. For them, Question Period is like the Garden of Gethsemane. It is the time when one is held to account. Anything which would change that would not only be unnecessary but it would cut into, and erode, some of the central principles of Parliament. However, when one looks at the changes about which we are speaking there may also be similar problems with respect to accountability. It must be asked: To what degree the law affects this place, as it does from time to time, in terms of keeping Government honest, open and responsible? It must also be asked: To what degree will the ability of a combined mass of Members coming together, whether in Question Period or in debate, be affected by these rule changes?
This is why the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) raised some serious cautions in his presentation. He raised them with respect to the functions of the committee and of the individual Member. He said that, in fact, we may be eroding or drawing down the capacity of Parliament to work as it should from time to time as the great crucible in which the issues of the day are exposed and in which the Government is held accountable.
Let me talk for a moment about the role of committees. 1 have been a member of many different committees and have seen how they operate. I believe that these rule changes fall short of achieving the objective that was established. Let me give some examples.
I thought that the committee in the last Parliament dealing with the problems of the handicapped played an invaluable role. It was chaired by the former Member for Don Valley West and was very much influenced by the former Member for Brandon-Souris, the late Walter Dinsdale, who died in office. He had a very sincere and incredible knowledge of this area. Those two Members were able to use that committee as a forum for drawing public attention to a series of issues that had been long neglected. As a Minister of that previous Government, I can testify as to how influential that committee was in putting those issues on the table and setting them on the agenda for Cabinet discussion. That committee achieved a remarkable record of success over three and four years of bringing forth legislation, regulation and initiatives on behalf of handicapped people.
Similarly, I can think back to my days in the provincial House when I was a member of the family law committee that worked for two years to overcome an incredible wealth of prejudice that had long existed in terms of property rights of men and women in marriage. Over a period of time, through the force of its public exposure, it was able to mobilize public opinion and eventually bring about major legislative change.
I also think of the recent action of the Joint Committee on Canada's International Relations, whose chairman is in the
February 13, 1986

House today. Last summer that committee served as a forum in the debate on star wars for a number of concerned Canadians. It gave them an opportunity to present their views and it ultimately mobilized public opinion, which obviously influenced the Government's decision about whether it should take part in star wars research.
These are issues in which parliamentary committees played an important role. They were able to fulfil that role because they had the ability to link with a high level of public identity and exposure. These committees were able to attract the attention of the media because of their partnership with the public on specific issues, which also mobilized the public constituency in the country.
I am concerned that there is nothing in these rule changes that will allow the new committee structure to provide for that kind of link with the public. One of the problems in the House of Commons is the incredible focus that is placed on Question Period. It is generally referred to as "show-biz time" because that is where all the media attention is focused. I defy Members to find any report of speeches made in the House or the work in committees reported in the local news, the national television news or even in the newspapers. It seems that Parliament has been turned on its head, and I suggest that the committee and these rule proposals have failed to address how to put Parliament back into its proper perspective as a debating forum rather than the show-biz arena with 45 minutes of comedy routines.
I understand the attraction of Question Period. Television has made the difference because the television audience does not enjoy talking heads, it enjoys conflict. That is why wrestling and other sports events are so popular; people like the one-on-one, hand-to-hand combat. To a great extent, Question Period has that quality.
I doubt very much whether people are educated or better informed by watching Question Period, because the question and response system is presently designed as a partisan form of game playing, with some rare exceptions. It is like a game show on television, competing for audiences during that particular time slot. This detracts from the role that Parliament should play in its committee and its debate on legislation.
We are concerned that the rule changes should not be implemented in an ad hoc manner but should reflect the broader perspective in order to make his place a far more relevant and significant institution for the debate of public issues. That is what I believe Canadians want, rather than relegating Parliament to the level of a game show or soap opera. It may be advantageous for attracting audiences, but ultimately Parliament must be a place for debate. I do not believe that the rule changes have addressed that issue at all.
We have heard much rhetoric about the role of committees but I suggest that those committees are only as good as their individual members. Furthermore, those members are only as good as their access to research, their staff and their ability to present informed questions about issues of importance to them.
Standing Orders
We know that the daily routine of Members of Parliament makes it difficult for them to find the time to do the necessary research to prepare for committees. They have far too many phone calls and constituency problems and caucus meetings to be able to obtain that substantial and useful information. Yet, the Member of Parliament is expected to become a paragon of wisdom under the new committee system and to take on new legislative initiatives and new levels of accountability. The rules do not take into account how the Member of Parliament will be able to get better access to research information and better staff resources. Unfortunately, this involves spending money and increasing the bureaucracy of Parliament.
I believe it is self-defeating to provide more responsibility to a Member of Parliament without providing the wherewithal to meet that responsibility. We are not taking a great leap forward if these reforms cannot be achieved because there is no capacity to meet those demands. That is why I believe parliamentary reform must take more than greater responsibility into account. We must also provide the means of meeting that responsibility.
What about the role of individual Members of Parliament representing their constituents? I was a Minister for almost five years, particularly in the portfolio of Employment and Immigration, in which there are numerous requests from Members of Parliament concerning immigration cases, unemployment insurance cases and job creation cases. Much of my time was spent acting almost like an ombudsman, trying to arbitrate the decisions of the bureaucracy brought to my attention by Members, as they legitimately should.
I ask all Hon. Members if they are satisfied that the system works effectively and they are able to deal effectively with the case work they receive in their constituency offices on the weekend? My colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis, said that if you are one of the Ministers' favourite sons or daughters, you may get a response. However, there are 282 Members in this House and all of us, to a greater or lesser degree, have individual cases of concern, whether it be immigration, pensions or unemployment insurance. What is the turn-around time? Three months? Four months? Some go on for six or seven months. Some immigration cases go on for a full year. I would suggest that if we are really concerned about how to achieve a greater role and responsibility for the individual Member, we have to recognize that a large part of the role is acting as a court of last resort for individuals frustrated by the bureaucracy. They cannot get access or fair decisions. The time honoured role of an MP is to provide that court of last resort and bring the issue to this Chamber or a Minister's attention.
However, the process, once the issue is brought here, is archaic and obsolete. Some Government Departments have two or three hundred correspondence secretaries handling these cases and telling people that, yes, the Minister has received their letter and we will get back. I do not have to go through it; any Minister knows exactly how the game is played. This is

February 13, 1986
Standing Orders
wrong. It is ineffective, and there are better ways of doing it. One technique we began to experiment with in the Department of Transport was establishing the office of Inspector General. That officer did not report to the Deputy Minister, but rather had direct access to the Minister and any level of the bureaucracy. Grievances and complaints could be raised in that way, and it would at the same time provide a focal point for Members of Parliament to refer these cases. That would be that persons' full-time job. When a particular problem in a given bureaucracy is identified, then they would have the right and responsibility to get it corrected. Why are we not doing that kind of thing to make the job of an individual Member of Parliament more successful?
I would just use the time remaining to say that I welcome with relief the opportunity of dealing with government appointments in committee. As Members of this House will know, we have been asking for close to five months to have the new trade negotiator, Mr. Reisman, appear before the committee so we can find out what his mandate is. We have been told consistently by the Prime Minister and others that that would not happen until these rules were established. Perhaps the time has now arrived and the day of reckoning will soon be here for Mr. Reisman and his points of view on trade. However, why do we have the power simply to hold hearings? I think we all realize that something like this is only significant when there is some power attached, some decision-making responsibility. The U.S. Senate has a very important function, it is called advise and consent. It is that ability to consent which is a very important bargaining point in establishing the rights of the legislative branch to hold the executive branch accountable. We have not gone that far. We have not given our committees the opportunity to restrain or restrict an appointment they consider to be totally unacceptable. Therefore, the process is, in part, meaningless. It may make certain information public but it will not give us the opportunity to ensure bad appointments can be withheld or stopped.
With those thoughts about where Parliament should go, I would say that the steps we are taking here are useful, but they are by no means the reforms which are necessary to make this place a modern place of work for all of us.

The extremely serious decision to deny a Member the privilege of occupying his seat should be taken by the House. Presently the Government House Leader must present a motion to expel a Member.
