speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I join with my colleagues in congratulating the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) on his remarks. I know him to be a hardworking Member and he has assiduously tried to fulfil his House, committee and constituency duties. I would like him, as a Member from Western Canada, to comment on the challenge to a Member in trying to cope with a series of legislative, standing and special committees, as well as task forces. This is in addition to the many other functions he has as Member of Parliament. How does he reconcile this with an increased workload for every Member of the House? Does he not think we should adopt the British system of queuing our legislation so that we have at the maximum seven or eight committees instead of 15 or 20 sometimes?
Without the staff you used to have.

Mr. Speaker, I thought for a moment our Whip was going to ask me how I, as a Liberal Member from western Canada, get by. It is a matter of sheer survival. In some ways the rules in which I am much more interested are those concerning the game laws in the Provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, in order to stay alive.
The Hon. Member raises an important point. About two weeks ago I had a conversation with a former Member of Parliament who represented a Winnipeg constituency back in the 1940s and 1950s. We bumped into each other. He was reminiscing about his days in the House and he talked about the time when Members would get on the train to go back to their constituency, having been in Ottawa for three or four months. The conclusion he came to was that modern-day communications have not been of great help to Members of Parliament, that they have in fact substantially increased our workload. We are overloading the system. I do not think that the human psyche, temperament or physiology are really built to handle all the responsibilities a Member of Parliament is expected to handle, to say nothing of a Minister of the Crown with administrative duties. We have to be a little more realistic and recognize that to do a good job you need the time and the
February 13, 1986

resources. It is foolish and foolhardy to think that somehow you can have an ever-expanding set of demands without having something to give. So what gives, the time you spend in your constituency? The time you spend with your family? That, quite frankly, is what usually gives. That is the real poison in the system. When you have a highly efficient and demanding Whip and a highly demanding set of committee responsibilities, you start shaving off time spent with your wife, children, and friends. You can no longer find extra moments for reflection and thinking. That must, after all, ultimately be the basis of strength.
We need a way of organizing the committee system to allow forward planning of one's time as well as much more careful consideration of travel requirements. There is a psychology that virtually every committee which is established must cover almost every city, town, village, and hamlet. If a committee does not go to a particular town, that town feels it has been ignored. As a result, there are many travelling road shows. Sometimes Members are expected to join three or four of those a year. Not only does the time spent in your office diminish, but the lack of personal time becomes a very major impairment.
In the consideration of these rules I strongly urge that one be more realistic and fair to Members of Parliament with regard to the responsibilities of committee work. If we are not going to do that, the least we can do is to ensure that Members have the resources to meet those demands, which resources we certainly do not have at the present time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to pursue the point of having numerous standing committees going about their work while, at the same time, there are legislative committees dealing with the same subject matter. That makes it very difficult for Members as it is impossible to be in two places at the same time. I am thinking of the de Havilland committee, for example, which had expertise available to it. Members who were interested in this very important subject were called upon to attend legislative committees dealing with subject matters related to trade, the high technology industry, and the aviation industry at the same time.
We would like the assurance of the Government that these new rules will be put into effect with some sensitivity to the fact that Members of Parliament cannot be in two places at the same time. If a committee studies a subject which is of importance to Members who are required to attend other committee meetings at that time, we would like the Government to postpone making its decision until that committee has reported. I know the Member has experience in these matters. What is his experience in terms of task forces and special committees and how they should relate to House business?

Mr. Speaker, as we have observed many times in this House, there are occasions when it becomes more like a three-ring circus than a serious legislative forum. Our Party Whip has put his finger on one of the serious flaws in
Standing Orders
this package of proposals. It is not realistic to believe that that can happen.
I suggest that there should be some machinery for administering the special legislative committees, whether through a committee of Whips or delegates from each caucus. If we are seriously talking about Members of Parliament having more control over their own destiny and time, it should be worked out in a way that is equitable and fair to all, rather than simply leaving it to the whims of the Government House Leader who is under pressure from his Cabinet colleagues to get legislation through. There must be some countervail to that. Perhaps a formal committee of the House, set up under the House Leaders, to administer the allocation of time for committees would be a proper way of ensuring that it is not abused.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate on the parliamentary reform proposals. I am sure that over the years, the experience I have acquired here in the House is quite considerable, but unfortunately, it would take more than fifteen or twenty minutes to elaborate on its various aspects.
However, I can inform my hon. colleagues that parliamentary life is a very complicated one, and that 1 am delighted the Government has finally decided to try to improve and enhance it, especially in terms of the role of the individual Member.
I must of course congratulate the members of the McGrath Committee, and especially the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), who so ably chaired the Committee's meetings, who produced this weighty and well-structured report, and who, I hope, will be ready to guide parliamentarians whenever further parliamentary reform will be necessary.
I have always maintained that the Hon. Member for St. John's East is a great Canadian parliamentarian, and he has demonstrated this, not only in the way he drafted and structured his report but also ever since he became a Member of the House of Commons. I have seen him at work for over twenty years. He is a lively speaker, a very active parliamentarian whose speeches are often colourful and always well-crafted. I would suggest his time and talents could be put to good use in areas other than his present concerns, and 1 think this would certainly benefit the House as a whole.
I wish him every success for the future, Mr. Speaker, and he has my full confidence and high esteem.
We talk about enhancing the role of the individual member, because that role has lost much of its effectiveness in this House.
If we take a brief look at the history of Parliament, I think that the British parliamentary system or at least the rules within the Commonwealth have formed the basis for the Canadian parliamentary system, except that over time, the Mother of Parliaments has introduced improvements and
10796

February 13, 1986
Standing Orders
reforms which we may have overlooked in Canada, although our Parliament is so closely modelled on that of Westminster.
I always tell my colleagues, and I was listening to my hon. friend from Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) with whom I have had the pleasure of sitting in this House for many years, I have always said that to any Member who has been sitting in Parliament for a number of years, the happiest day of his life as a Member is the night of his election when, in the middle of an enthusiastic crowd, he is on cloud nine, with music and dancing and a general euphoria all around. It is absolute heaven.
However, after the enthusiasm of the election campaign fades and he buys a new suit to pose for the cameras at his swearing in, his first session in Parliament begins.
I think that this Member, now sitting in his seat, probably lost in a single week all his illusions about his role as a Member in the House of Commons. The very same Member, who during his election campaign said what he was going to do and how he was going to make Parliament sit up and what he was going to tell the people who are responsible for forming the Government. Now all of a sudden he feels useless, and his feelings of inferiority will become harder and harder to hide, and that is why over the years, we have seen many legitimate complaints by newly elected members who become frustrated with the role they have to play in Parliament.
Today, being a parliamentarian is very exciting. It is a very important task but it is also very frustrating. There are a number of reasons for this, Mr. Speaker. First of all, there is the whole matter of the constraints put on the Member by his political party. Allegiance, the convention of confidence, and the structuring of Government Members all mean that these Members can do absolutely nothing unless they bow to those constraints. A Member may not, for whatever reason, vote against his party, especially if he is on the Government side, unless he wants to lay himself open to severe disciplinary action or even suspension from his party.
I can tell you that during the years I sat in this House I had occasions to vote against my Government on certain issues which were very important to my region and the riding I represent. There was some knuckle-rapping all right, but 1 was not alone, four of five Members from the National Capital Region did the same, a gesture which was then described as being odious. But I must say that things would be different if Members had more leeway, especially when a problem crops up in a region; the problem might be solved through a private Member's Bill, all the more so if the Member has been able to convince his colleagues that it will benefit not only that region but the country as a whole. I think that the Member's role would be immediately enhanced, and he would be able to make Canada a better country to live in because he would then be
echoing the aspirations of the great population of Canada from sea to sea.
Well, we do not have that much leeway. More often than not the Member feels quite powerless, he cannot even have a railway crossing removed even after campaigning on that issue in his riding. You are practically helpless, and all you can do is to attempt through a hard lobbying campaign to convince certain Ministers to make the change you are fighting for to improve the life of your fellow citizens or your constituents. But even that does not work out, Mr. Speaker, because the shackles are still there, the technocrats wield unbelievable power. Even when it comes to drafting legislation and deciding what should be in it you cannot get to first base, you are at their mercy for the simple reason that the technocrat is the one who decides the kind of political direction to be taken with respect to certain problems in Canada.
I am quite pleased to learn that Members will have more power, particularly in committees which are, in my view, the backbone of the House of Commons. The House of Commons is nothing more that a forum where bills are debated, analysed and screened as much as possible, a place where the remarks and views of Members may or may not lead to improved legislation.
I said earlier, I think that it is time for us to find a way, and I am very glad that this is being done, to make the role of Members of Parliaments more relevant, because we have all had this feeling of uselessness in the House of Commons and often in the committees. Even though we say to our constituents that we must be visible, that the role of a Member of Parliament is to be visible and present in his constituency, we know quite well that the House of Commons sits about 10 months each year, five days a week. How can a Member of Parliament be attuned to the needs and demands of his constituents and his region? It is impossible, Mr. Speaker! This is why, as statistics show, many Members are elected to the House of Commons, but few remain for long, maybe not through any fault of their own, but because they did not have the time to do the job of a real Member of Parliament, which is simply to be an ombudsman and a representative of his constituents in the federal Parliament. They are not able to do so because they spend all their time in Ottawa, because, often, they have to move their family to Ottawa, because they do not have any time to go back to their constituency. After four or five years, they are defeated simply because they have been completely cut off from reality and from the aspirations of their own constituents. This certainly shows a weakness in our parliamentary system. When we bring about reforms, we have to be very carefull not to be in too much of a hurry for the simple reason that reform often requires other reforms, but those are not brought about and this often unbalances the whole system. I am very happy that the role of Members will be increased, but I am really anxious to see how this will be done because the recommendations of the Committee have not
February 13, 1986

all been implemented. I hope that many others will be because it would benefit Canadian Parliament. I also hope that Members of Parliament will regain the role they had early in the Confederation, that of representatives of the people. We have become second-class citizens inside this House. We all legislate by lobby, by consensus, by Gallup poll, through the technocrats, through those who provide guidance and even political advice to the Government. We should give more influence and more relevance to the Member of Parliament so that when we legislate, it is in the best interests of Canadians. Perhaps one day, Mr. Speaker, we should perhaps even stop trying to legislate during four or five years and try to go back to improve the statutes which have already been adopted to correct the abuses and restrictions that some of them may have imposed on some groups in our society. In think that, in this way, everyone will take part in the development of Canadian legislation and will be happy to have been able to do so. It is essential for the Member of Parliament to regain his former role, and in this way, we can build a better Canada.
We will have fewer protests, fewer claims, because Canadians will be happier about the situation.
In the years 1930, 1933, 1935, 1940, and I could go as far back as the early years of Confederation, Parliament was not sitting ten months a year, Mr. Speaker. It used to sit three or four months. Perhaps, what with a larger population, greater organization, Parliament can do with six or seven months of session.
But we cannot govern Canadians by legislating ten months a year. If we legislate without knowing the aspirations of the people-and the aspirations of the Canadian people are only expressed here, in Parliament, through their representatives, Members from the 282 constituencies that make up Canada's electoral map.
I tell you in a non-partisan way that many Members realize their uselessness in this House because they have not been given a sufficiently important role.
I appreciate the intention to increase the efficiency and role of the committees, Mr. Speaker. But there again, it is recommended that 26 committees be created, I believe. There are 18 standing comittees, and the other ones, with seven members. This meant that quite a number of Members will still be sitting on those committees. If we add the legislative committees, and God knows how many legislative committees may be sitting at the same time, it then means that you are keeping almost all of Parliament busy, excluding the Ministers! There is nobody left in the House, because everybody is kept busy elsewhere ... You might say this is hypothetical, because all committees cannot sit at the same time. I agree. But I am also sure that if we had the facilities needed to have Members sitting, and I am talking about rooms that could be made
Standing Orders
available to committees, there would be days when 25 to 30 committees would be sitting at one and the same time.
Mr. Speaker, this is why I am very pleased to see that the Member's role will be enhanced, "revalorise" in the French version, and I like the word very much because it means the Member was not of a very great value before we came to use the word "revaloriser". I am therefore very happy that the term was used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), if I am not mistaken, and that the House will become what it should always have been, an essential body for governing all Canadians by making laws, drawing up laws that meet the aspirations of the Canadian people.
And if we do not reach that goal, if again Members are prevented from fully playing their roles-I heard speeches, and almost everybody is singing the same song, it is absolutely vital to enhence the private Member's role.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I heard among other things, remarks concerning the suspension of Members. It is my view that Members will have their way because this is part of parliamentary life. There are people who are more aggressive than others. There are people who feel more strongly than others that they are being wronged, for the simple reason that they are under heavier attack or because problems come up in their constituencies and apparently the Government cannot or will not listen to them.
1 even read in the committee report that the intention was, that it was being considered that it might be better to pass legislation in this House to fine them, like when you go through a red light.
It should be realized, as this has been suggested, that Members are grownups, and responsible people, the proof being that they were elected. When we are told that Members are not very relevant, it must be kept in mind that there are 282 of us from all across Canada. If you divide our total population of 26 million people by this number, I think it shows that each one of us represents a very substantial segment of the Canadian population. Well, Mr. Speaker, that was the modest contribution I wanted to make on the subject of these proposals for parliamentary reform, which I hope will be put into effect as soon as possible-time tell how important these reforms will have been-and if they are not, I hope they will be discarded without further ado.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a very brief question to the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Isabelle). In the course of my research on the subject of the Speaker's authority to name a Member and to suspend him from the service of the House for the remainder of the day, I was able to find only one instance in the history of this House. It was in 1942, when the Member for Laval-Deux Montagnes was

February 13, 1986
The Royal Assent
suspended from the House for the entire day, and a second time for seven days. Never in the history of this House, either before or after, as the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer is aware, has this disciplinary measure been used more than once. I wonder... I am not sure whether the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer was for or against the five-day suspension. Could he tell us exactly where he stands on these additional powers of the Speaker? Does he think it is putting the Speaker in a rather embarrassing situation, when we realize that the Government has never used this particular measure?

Of course, Mr. Speaker, I think the question asked by my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) is both important and delicate. I would not want the Speaker of the House to experience problems in the discharge of his difficult duties, but the one thing I can say for sure-and I said so when some Hon. Members showed aggressiveness for reasons I would rather not delve into-is that a temperamental Member may get carried away at times, but I do not see why anyone should be thrown out or suspended for five days. 1 think that is more than anyone can say about a Member who has been suspended for five days, but I would rather see him pay a fine. I would like that to be left to the discretion of the Chair, we should maintain our time-honoured tradition whereby the Member is suspended for the rest of the day, but no more.
On debate, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker).
Mr. Speaker, 1 have just a few comments to make, because I understand someone else wishes to participate.
1 apologize for interrupting the Hon. Member, but at this point I should like to give notice of The Royal Assent.

Order. I have the honour to inform the House that a communication has been received as follows:
Government House Ottawa
February 13, 1986 Sir:
I have the honour to inform you that the Honourable Antonio Lamer, Puisne Judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, in his capacity as Deputy Governor General, will proceed to the Senate Chamber today, the 13th day of February, 1986, at 5.45 p.m., for the purpose of giving Royal Assent to certain Bills.
Yours sincerely.
Leopold H. Amyot,
Secretary to the Governor General.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. This being Friday-
It is Thursday!
This being Thursday, I was going to ask Your Honour how you pronounce p-u-i-s-n-e.
I was going to ask the Hon. Member the same question. Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate.

Mr. Speaker, before you interrupted me I was about to suggest that one of the first changes that should be made to the rules of procedure is to have a permanent Speaker, but that came off my time, I think.
Let me be very clear. If the Hon. Member feels that way, it will not come off his time.

Just a few words, Mr. Speaker. I say in all honesty that I think one of the primary things that should take place in a legislature under the British parliamentary system in the 1980s is certainly to have a full and complete debate on the proposition of having a permanent Speaker. Perhaps that is one of the two important subjects that should be dealt with in a debate in this Chamber such as this.
The other thing that should be dealt with is a subject that some Members do not want to deal with, and it is this. I was listening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) the other day when he said that he would like to restore the power to Members of Parliament in this Chamber. He said that he would like to bring this House of Commons into the 20th century in the great British tradition. The other part of the question that has to be dealt with, if that is what the Prime Minister wants to do, is, first and foremost, that Members of Parliament will have to allow an impartial body exterior to this Chamber to have the power to make changes in the procedures of this House.
Members here in this House and members of the committee would say, "Well, that's a terrible thing to suggest". Not so, Mr. Speaker. If you were going to follow the British tradition or the traditions of any legislature under the British parliamentary system you would, first and foremost, have to accept that as being necessary for complete change, because that is exactly what the other legislatures-if I can refer to them generally-have done. They are Parliaments, but they are more than Parliaments-from the French word to speak- because they do more than that, they legislate. That is their primary function. How is that accomplished, Mr. Speaker? It was accomplished, first of all, by that body of Parliamentarians saying, "If we only allow ourselves to be restricted by our own suggestions, then we will never change and we will never get to the point where this Parliament become a legislative body". When the Prime Minister said, "Well, now, we would
February 13, 1986

like to get back to what the British parliamentary system was in this country", what he would have to be suggesting, in order to do that, to do what the British and the Australians have done, is to do what any legislature has done, and that is, to have an outside body recommend and implement rule changes in this legislature.
The other aspect is the question of a permanent Speaker. I think that all Members will agree that we have been particularly fortunate in this country over the last 10, 12, or 15 years. 1 believe that at any moment in time during that period either political Party could have instituted the position of permanent Speaker and there would not have been objections from the other side of the Chamber. I do not think there would be objections, because if you examine the role of the Speaker and what the Speaker is asked to do in this particular legislature, it is to try to provide a mix of customs in this House supported by the Standing Orders, the traditions of rules and procedures, and then you find, and I am sure you will agree, that he is in a particularly precarious situation. I would like to read into the record Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, Fourth Edition, 1958, at page 147: It reads as follows:
A question oral or written must not: be ironical, rhetorical, offensive, or contain ephithet, innuendo, satire or ridicule.
That's rule number one. Now, let us take number two:
A question oral or written must not: be trivial, vague or meaningless.
If that weren't enough, it says:
A question oral or written must not multiply, with slight variations, a similar question on the same point.
Then you have to look at the next one:
A question oral or written must not: repeat in substance a question already answered, or to which an answer has been refused.
An answer that has been refused, that's about all the answers you get here, the answers that are refused. Then it
says:
A question oral or written must not: inquire whether statements made in a newspaper are true.
Now just imagine, Mr. Speaker, you have not really been doing your job, have you?
No.

It continues.
A question oral or written must not: contain an expression of opinion.
Mr. Speaker, you are supposed to rule 90 per cent of the questions out of order. A question cannot be hypothetical or contain inferences. Then it cannot be framed so as to suggest its own answer. It cannot refer discourteously to a friendly foreign country. It cannot contain or imply charges of a personal character. It cannot relate to matters which passed outside the walls of the House, or relate to any Bill or motion before the House. It cannot ask the Government's opinion on matters of policy. It cannot ask what advice the Minister proposes to give the Crown. It cannot seek information about matters which are in their nature secret, such as decisions or proceedings of the Cabinet.
Standing Orders
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you would have to agree that you have broken every single rule in Beauchesne in this Chamber. I suppose, Mr. Speaker, what is on your mind is, "You, Member for Gander-Twillingate, you have broken them yourself in asking the questions". Mr. Speaker has just said, in case it was not picked up, that I should read the section about relevance in debate. If I cannot read from Beauchesne on the rule changes I would like to know what is relevant and what is not in this debate. Mr. Speaker, I could go on. If we look at our rules of procedures-
Go on.

Go on? Okay. Here's a good one on page 5 of the same edition:
No member shall walk out of or cross the House, or make any noise or disturbance.
Then:
When a member is speaking, no member shall pass between him and the Chair, nor interrupt him ...
The next one reads as follows:
When the House adjourns the members shall keep their seats until Mr. Speaker has left the Chair.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if you were to follow the rules in Beauchesne that you should be following as the Speaker of this House then, of course, Mr. Speaker, you would have some difficulty with our traditions, with our customs, but you have to provide a mix. It is a very subjective position. You make a value judgment, Mr. Speaker, with practically everything that happens in this Chamber. As to the proposition about making rule changes for Members of this House, 1 would like to disagree with that very briefly. The rule changes to be made in this Chamber are not for Members of Parliament, they should be for the people of Canada. They should be for the Parliament of Canada. Members of Parliament come and go, as you know. They are here one year and gone the next. The turnover here is 30, 40 per cent with each election. Some Cabinet Ministers think that they have not been appointed, they have been anointed for life. Certain Members of Parliament actually believe that. The changes to be made in this Chamber should be for the benefit of the people of Canada for all time and for the benefit of Parliament. There is an overriding principle here that we agree with in opposition. That basic principle of our democracy is that a Government is elected to govern.
How profound.

The Minister is saying that that is profound, but sometimes it is forgotten that a Government is elected to govern. Therefore, the entire principle of our democracy is that the Parliament of Canada has only one function, and that is, to make the Government accountable to the people.
With the flow of legislation and the interruption in actions of the Government, the Parliament of Canada-

He's really winding up.

February 13, 1986
Standing Orders

The Hon. Member is saying that 1 am getting wound up here. It is a very important subject, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you will agree with me.
We have to remember that the Government has to govern. The Parliament is not here to prevent the Government from governing but to make the Government accountable to the people of Canada through Parliament, and that is the main point.
How do we go about making the Government of Canada accountable to the people of Canada? It has to be done through Parliament. A Minister should never be able to rise in the House to make an announcement on a policy change or change through Order in Council that will affect people throughout the country with no accountability to the people of Canada.
Nowhere in our rules of procedure or in the operation of Parliament does it say that a Minister has to answer to anything. Not in Question Period, in a committee or elsewhere does a Minister have to answer to the people of Canada on a policy.
Election day.

The hon. gentleman reminded me of election day. If that is the only way Ministers can be accountable, what is the purpose of Parliament?
I would return to my original suggestion that we look at other legislatures which are under the British parliamentary system. There we see a system which is completely contrary to the one which has evolved here. The actual action of accountability takes place in various forms, but it certainly does not take place in a chamber such as this. It takes place in committees that can originate their own terms of reference and in customs that have been developed in those legislatures.
If Hon. Members were to watch Question Period occurring in another legislature under the British parliamentary system, they would see that Government Members are just as critical of the Government as Opposition Members. You know that to be a fact, Mr. Speaker. Because of that, the tradition of the Speaker being able to recognize first a Government Member, then an Opposition Member, another Government Member and then another Opposition Member evolved. Is that not correct, Mr. Speaker? Of course it is. That would certainly not work in this Parliament with Government Members who have planted questions that waste the time of the people of Canada.
Hopefully we will arrive at such a stage one day. However, what I have to say is very basic and it is that if we really want to change the rules and procedures of Parliament, we should allow an outside body to make recommendations. It may be terrible that I am suggesting this to Members of Parliament, but I am only doing what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said he was doing the other day. I am looking at the great traditions of our parliamentary system. We should allow an outside group to make recommendations on the condition that they be implemented by Parliament.
Let it not be forgotten that our function is to make the Government accountable to the people of Canada. Members of Parliament should realize that they are only here for a short period of time. Hopefully, opposition Members will be here a lot longer than government Members.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on the matter the Hon. Member raised regarding the Speaker. While you are in the chair, Mr. Speaker, this is a good opportunity to
do so.
I am one of the Members of the House who have perhaps had some run ins with the Chair in the last couple of weeks when posing questions.

speechtext: Run outs.

I do not like the fact that some of the newer Members of the House are running to the press with critical comments about the Speaker. I do not think that that is the way Parliamentarians should handle things and 1 do not think that that is the way we should treat the Speaker of the House because the Speaker is our servant.
Perhaps Hon. Members will say that I should not talk about this because I have had some run ins with the Speaker, and it is true. However, I have never been publicly critical of the Speaker and I never will. Quite frankly, there have been occasions on which my supplementary questions have been too long.
No, no.

It is true that we should be cutting back on them.
The Hon. Member made some remarks about a permanent Speaker. I do not think that we should have a permanent Speaker. I think we should choose our Speaker from among us because the Speaker has to be part of the House and part of the living House. There is a danger that a permanent Speaker would become a bureaucrat on the job.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member who just spoke and who received the support of some Hon. Members has just disagreed with the most respected authorities in the area of political science and parliamentary review in the British Commonwealth and certainly in North America-
Name one, George. One author.

The Minister says that I should name one. I suggest that in his spare time, he read the journal entitled The Parliamentarian or any of the recent literature-and by recent, I mean written in the last 20 years-that has been written on the subject.
It is interesting to see that a Cabinet Minister is disagreeing with me. Now I think I really have a point. It would be like

arguing that the Officers of the Table should only enjoy tenure of office while Parliament is in session and be dismissed when Parliament is not in session. That is the same thing, no matter how we look at it. The more one reads about it and studies it, the more one realizes that there is only one solution to the problem.
Oh, oh!

It is not a problem, but I think, Mr. Speaker, you would have to agree that it is funny that the same Cabinet Minister who is disagreeing with me now is the very person who disagreed with having an outside body propose changes to our procedures in Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Hon. Member could assist me as I pore through those learned journals by giving me the name of one author so that 1 could find the relevant material more quickly.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member does not realize this, but while I was the Chief Clerk-
Name one.
Just listen now. While I was the Chief Clerk of a provincial legislature-
You wrote them.

-and the Secretary of the Canadian Branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, I did, under my own name, write an excellent article in The Parliamentarian, and I would recommend it to the hon. gentleman at any time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House to express my support, of course, for reform generally and the principle of reform, and if I am somewhat hesitant to declare my support for the amendments as submitted, it is because I have some reservations, and I think they are quite justified, about three or four points which I consider very important. Mr. Speaker, the main goal of these reform proposals should be to enhance the role and powers of each Member of the House, especially the backbencher.
Mr. Speaker, I think that to a certain extent we are just deluding ourselves and others by claiming that the individual Member or backbencher will have greater powers as a result of reforms like the proposals before the House today. When I say we are deluding ourselves, I say this because I have been sitting in the House for thirteen years, and the British parliamentary system is designed in terms of parliamentary groups and not in terms of individuals. And in this House, it is the parliamentary groups,-the group of the party in power and the Opposition party groups,-who conduct the exchanges in the House and debate the questions of the day. The role of the
Standing Orders
individual Member is, as we said earlier, to hold the Government accountable to the Canadian people, and that forms the basis of our democratic system which harks back to the British system and British traditions. So when we say that we are going to enhance the powers of the individual member, I think we are in fact deluding ourselves, and perhaps dangerously so, because in my view, we as Members of this House, as full Members, have the power to use the rules and traditions and to do whatever else we can in the way of influencing the order of business in the House, to obtain from the Government the accountability we need to be able to carry out our task.
That being said, Mr. Speaker-I said so earlier, and I know I do not have much time to repeat this-I would simply tell the House that as Whip of my Party, the Liberal Party and the Official Opposition, I did run into some problems with the provisional Standing Orders of last June. There were quite a few difficulties concerning legislative committees, for instance. I think it was necessary to review the legislative committee system over the past six or eight months, and we were unable to change or modify this approach because both sides were reluctant to do so and the Standing Orders made no provision for this.
So I see in this reform an opportunity to ask the Government-to demand, if need be-to guarantee that during the ten month period when these Standing Orders will be in force we in the Opposition will be able, with the Government guarantee, to reconsider now and then some of the measures to be adopted which might indeed need to be adjusted as we go along. Therefore I think that if the Government is in good faith, if it is prepared to give us the assurance that it will listen to us and perhaps even take part in improving the rules or helping smooth out some of the difficulties, then I would consider that a very constructive step.
The second point, Mr. Speaker, and it has been debated at length over the last three days, is the question of allowing the Chair to suspend a Member for five days after he has been called to order for the second, third or fourth time and been named by the Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, I have no problem with the Chair's power to name a member once and ask him or her to withdraw from the House. But I have quite a problem with the additional power which you would have to exclude a member from the House for five consecutive days. I suggested earlier that this change is not in line with our practices, customs and traditions either as the House of Commons or Government. 1 just cannot see why you should be given this power or authority.
Mr. Speaker, 1 see that that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is back. I am told that he is about to make a few remarks. I am quite willing to defer to him at any time. Of course, I could certainly elaborate on the problems which I foresee concerning for instance the Private Members' Hour. I suggest adjustments will have to be made so that every Private Member's Bill be dealt with equally and equitably.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the points which have been raised during the course of this debate. I wish to congratulate every Member who participated in it. I think it has been a full debate, which was asked for by many Members of the House. We have had the benefit of hearing a number of points of view.
As I mentioned earlier, I have had the opportunity of consulting with my opposition House Leader colleagues about the way in which we could respond to the matters which have been raised in this debate. As a result of those discussions, we have been able to arrive at a consensus. There is a disposition to conclude the debate at this time.
I would like to indicate at the outset that 1 will be seeking consent at the time that the package is adopted to have the following changes deemed to be adopted in the proposed Standing Orders. I think the best way of doing this is to read them. They state:
That the proposed amendments to the Standing Orders laid upon the Table, Thursday, February 6, 1986. (Sessional Paper No. 331-7/37AO) be amended
(a)	at page 1646 of the Votes and Proceedings of February 6, 1986, by striking out the lines thereon relating to Standing Order 16 and substituting the following therefor:
"(6) (a) The Speaker shall be vested with the authority to maintain order by naming individual members for disregarding the authority of the Chair and, without resort to motion, ordering their withdrawal for the remainder of that sitting, notwithstanding Standing Ordere 8".
(b)	at pages 1649 and 1650 of the Votes and Proceedings of February 6, 1986, by striking out proposed Standing Order 38(2) and substituting the following therefor:
"(2) Unless previously disposed of, selected public bills at the second reading stage or selected motions shall receive not more than five hours of consideration and, unless previously disposed of, an item having been once considered, shall be dropped to the bottom of the order of precedence and again considered only when it reaches the top of the said order.
Provided that, unless otherwise disposed of, at not later than fifteen minutes before the end of the time provided for the consideration of the said item any proceedings then before the House shall be interrupted and every question necessary to dispose of the selected motion or of the selected bill at the 2nd stage, shall be put forthwith and successively without further debate or amendment."
The effect of those changes will be evident from the document itself, inasmuch as they deal with two aspects of concern that have been raised. One was to assure that in terms of Private Members' Business there will be no arbitrary curtailment of the time available for discussion of Private Members' Business unless it is done by the consent of the House. I believe that is a fair and reasonable proposition. We will then make sure that we will be guided by the wish of the House with respect to the length of that debate.
The second is one which, I think is fair to say, I have have spoken to you about. You indicated that you were quite happy and satisfied with respect to the change. We are removing any second naming offence under the rules of the House of Commons. We will proceed on the basis that you will have the power and ability to name, as recommended by the committee chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath).
That is the effect of those two items. These changes address the concerns raised during the debate with respect to the extended expulsion of Members for breaches of order and with respect to the length of time to be provided for the consideration of Private Members' Business.
Members have also raised concerns with respect to the length of time to be provided for statements under S.O. 22, the selection of report stage amendments and the number of questions that Members will be permitted to place on the Order Paper. The provisional Standing Orders are being brought forward on an experimental basis for a trial period because we are all aware of the fact that there will be a need from time to time to modify or make improvements in the
February 13, 1986

rules as we gain experience with their operation. I simply want to reiterate the comments that I made in opening this debate, that the Government will carefully monitor the workings of the House rules and I, in co-operation with the Opposition House Leaders, will not wait until the end of the trial period to make any necessary changes. Instead, in the true spirit of reform, we will attempt to fine-tune the rules from time to time to ensure the success of this experiment.
Some Members have suggested that information about Members travelling on Government-sponsored business should be required to be disclosed to the register of Member's travel. I thought, at this point, that it might be useful to remind Members that the public disclosure of that information is currently required under the provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act. In order to conform to the provisions of the Act an Order in Council is required to be passed every time that a Member travels on a Government-sponsored trip. Upon passage of the Order in Council, the information is made public.
I know that Members on all sides of the House have raised concerns about the matter of monitoring legislative committees and the demands on Members' time. The House Leaders have discussed this matter and we have agreed to monitor committee activities on an ongoing basis to ensure the smooth scheduling of committee work. We will undertake this work as part of our regular negotiations on the legislative agenda.
In summary, I believe that with the changes that I have outlined and with the commitment of all House Leaders to co-operate to ensure the success of reform, the House is now ready to proceed with the proposed Standing Orders and with what I believe to be a very important turning point in the development of the Canadian House of Commons.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I opened the debate a few days ago on behalf of the Official Opposition, I said that as far as I and my colleagues were concerned, if we and especially the Government were serious about the role of the private Member, then the test would be the extent to which the Government was willing to listen to what private Members, particularly in the opposition, had to say in the course of that debate on the Government's formal and latest proposal for amending the Standing Orders.
During the course of that debate private Members, particularly on the Opposition side, raised a number of concerns. Principal among those concerns were the ones enumerated by the Government House Leader in his statement. Of course, some of these concerns were greater than others and those which appear to be of immediate concern are reflected in the Minister's proposal for amending the draft Standing Orders.
With respect to the others, I must say that as far as we are concerned, the changes in the rules are very much on trial. The period of 10 months in which they will go into operation is not necessarily, in our view, just the first step in making them permanent. We will be watching the entire package very closely, not only the measures the Government House Leader says he will keep under review. The test of any organization,
Standing Orders
whether it be a legislative body or a country, for that matter, is the way minorities in that system are treated.
Therefore, we believe that the litmus test for assessing the way these rule changes work is the way individual Members of Parliament on the Opposition side fare under the rule changes both as individuals and particularly as members of organized Party groups. As I said in my remarks a few days ago, our system is not based on Government facing off with private Members but on Government facing off with Members organized in Parties. We believe the litmus test will be not only how this system works for us as individual Members in Opposition but, in particular, how it works for us as Opposition Parties.
Therefore, it is important that we be ready to assess how it is proceeding and to make changes as soon as problems are seen to arise. We will be assessing how ready the Government will be to respond to our concerns. In particular, we will be looking to see how effectively the House Leaders, as part of their ongoing work, are able to monitor the operations of the committee system, particularly the legislative committees, to avoid the conflicts and proliferation which have disturbed so many of us.
As well, Mr. Speaker, and I am coming to a conclusion, the Government House Leader properly pointed out that travel by Members of the House on Government business has to be recorded and disclosed under the House of Commons Act through Orders in Council. However, I invite him to work with us on a system whereby these Orders in Council, as a matter of course, are brought into the hands of the Registrar of Members' travel so that they will be as available for inspection as the material which Members file directly with respect to other kinds of travel.
Having said all that, I want to conclude by stating that what we have seen today is very much the result of all of us, especially the Government, taking into account what was said during this debate by Members of Parliament, particularly on the Opposition side. I am glad to see this response and I look forward to the test period for these rules being fruitful and useful. However, I say to the Government: Please do not think that this is for us merely a first step toward making anything permanent. These rules are very much on trial and the test for us will be how fairly we see these rules waching for us as members of the Opposition, both individually and in groups.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak twice in this debate. However, let me say simply that I think what you are seeing here today is the result of parliamentary reform. It is the change in attitude which is necessary if we are to make parliamentary reform acceptable to everyone. I have no doubt at all, if the mood which prevails now continues throughout the year, that we will resolve whatever problems arise. We will find a way to accommodate the needs of the Government, taking into account the needs and desires of the Opposition. I look forward to the challenge of the new rules. I hope they work in the way which the committee that worked so hard to draft them intended them to work. I

It certainly would be my wish, and I am sure that of the other two House Leaders, that that would be the case. I look forward to the end of this year, when we are asked to review them, to a review which may require some further adjustment but which will make these the permanent rules governing the actions and efforts of Members of the House of Commons.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING CHILD ABUSE
speechtext:
that Bill C-261, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (child abuse), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to have this opportunity, finally, to present to the House of Commons Bill C-261 for the purpose of giving it second reading. The purpose of the Bill and this opportunity is to draw the attention of the House of and the public to the serious concern we have as Parliamentarians and that we should have as Canadians about the seemingly rising problem of child abuse.
I would hope that the utilization of the material in the Bill will heighten the awareness of the House and of the various committees associated with it to the problem of child abuse and to the fact that it is time that we as Members of Parliament did something and took some action.
I understand there is a disposition at some time during the proceedings to move a motion to have the Bill withdrawn and to move the substance of the Bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I am also aware that because of the Royal Assent that has just been given our allotted time is shortened somewhat. I hope all those who wish to speak on the matter will bear that in mind when making their comments.
1 would like to give a brief background of how 1 became aware and concerned about the substance of the Bill. On my arrival in Ottawa as a Member of Parliament some seven and a half years ago I noticed what seemed to me to be the
Criminal Code
alarming incidence of reports on child abuse contained in the national newspapers. This Bill is my response to the issue.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it took a substantial amount of time to prepare the Bill after much research and consultation with fellow Parliamentarians and with people who were and continue to this day to stress the importance of dealing with this serious issue.
I would like to pay tribute to the office of the Law Clerk, who co-operated substantially in the drafting of the Bill, and to the Parliamentary Counsel. In addition, 1 would like to thank my parliamentary assistant, Miss Pike, who spent countless hours helping me in the development of the Bill and working with me to ensure that this day finally came to fruition.
It is also appropriate at this time to state unequivocally that the Badgley Report contributed significantly to the drafting of the Bill and to the terms and conditions of it. I want to acknowledge the efforts of the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) who participated not only on the Badgley Commission but who has been a ceaseless and tireless worker in her efforts to ensure that the plight of helpless children is brought to the attention of the proper authorities.
I hope that at the end of my remarks the House will recognize that I am simply requesting that it take the material in the Bill into consideration. It is not perfect. It does have some warts and I recognize that but the purpose of the Bill is to make the House and the country aware of the concern we share.
I anticipate that sending the subject matter to the committee by withdrawing the Bill will accomplish the concern expressed in the the Bill itself.
As the Badgley Report indicates, the special legal status of children is based primarily on three considerations: first, the special needs of children who, by reason of their age and immaturity, need the care and guidance of others in order to develop into healthy, responsible adults; second, the substantial vulnerabilities of children to persons older and in many cases more powerful than they; and, third, the actual or presumed incapacity of children to perform legal acts of daily life.
Child abuse can range from being exposed to sexual intercourse, to deprivation of basic needs and to death. There are three main types of abuse: physical abuse or battering, failure to thrive or neglect, usually involving food or water deprivation or inadequate hygiene, and sexual abuse involving incest, violent molestation and pornographic exploitation.
Child abuse knows no bounds. It cuts across all economic, religious and geographic levels. The myth should be dispelled that it happens in only low-income, uneducated families. The facts speak differently.
Child abuse, both sexual assault and battering, is still largely a whispered crime. Many people choose to ignore that it happens or choose to make excuses for it. More people are beginning to address the issue, but for the most part, victims live in an aura of silence and fear.

February 13, 1986
Criminal Code

Mr. Speaker, the basic principle should be that everyone must be able to live in complete security in his own home. The home should not be a place where there is violence or sexual abuse.

Statistical evidence from all regions in Canada indicate an alarming increase in child abuse cases coming to the attention of the authorities. The question exists: Do the rising figures show a growing rate of child abuse, or are they a reflection of growing awareness of the problems that exist and a willingness to bring these incidents to the attention of the authorities? The secrecy of the crimes make the proportions of the problem an unknown quantity.
The concept of child abusers as strangers largely underestimates the type of people who abuse children. Abuse is inflicted by relatives, such as parents, aunts, uncles, cousins, by people in guardian positions such as step-parents, legal guardians, or by those in a position of trust, such as baby-sitters, teachers, family friends and acquaintances.
Abuse manifests itself in a wide variety of social, psychological and behavioural ways. An abused child may suffer from an inability to form social relations. It may have difficulty relating to authority. It may suffer from child-parent conflict, have a poor self-image, become suicidal, suffer a variety of health problems, and even suffer sexual diseases. It can develop phobias, have eating problems, suffer mental health problems, have trouble sleeping, turn to drugs or alcohol, become aggressive and assaultive. Unfortunately, some of these problems can continue throughout a lifetime no matter how much counselling the child may receive afterwards.
The Committee on Sexual Offences Against Children was established to examine the adequacy of our laws to protect children from sexual abuse and to offer recommendations on our legal shortcomings. The report offered specific recommendations to be implemented in the law as well as revisions that would clean up outmoded concepts or gender discrimination. The findings of the Badgley Report were influential in the development of the sexual abuse portion of Bill C-261.
The report indicated that one out of every two females and one out of every three males are at some point in their lives victims of unwanted sexual activity. In a substantial number of cases, this occurs under the age of 18 years. The Badgley Report indicated the following:
There is no basis for the alleged harmlessness of unwanted sexual acts committed against children or for the belief that most of the offenders are harmless individuals. We have found that young victims are encouraged, seduced and intimidated by sexual offenders. Some of these children sustain physical injuries. Many experience enduring emotional and social harms. Our findings clearly show that these children have special needs and vulnerabilities which must be recognized and protected by the criminal law and that existing provisions do not adequately accomplish these purposes.
The principal victims of sexual offences are children and young people, and females are twice as often victims as are males. In the majority of cases a sexual offence against a
person occurs before that person is 18 years of age. The age of battered children is dropping, and pre-school children are particularly vulnerable to abuse as they are not subject to the watchful eye of teachers or of other authorities.
The Badgley Report provided alarming figures regarding the relationship of children and youth to their offenders. Almost one in four of the sexual offences was committed by a person prominent in the child's life or to whom the child was vulnerable. About three of every five offences were committed by persons the victim either knew well or was acquainted with.
Badgley also reported that young persons were at greater risk from blood relations and persons in positions of trust than from other persons. The greater proportion of sexual offences committed by persons in a position of trust was against a child under the age of 12. A full 86 per cent of offences by a person in a position of trust concerned a child 11 years of age or under.
Reports of child abuse are growing. Last year, in Ontario, reported cases jumped by 19 per cent. This figure includes five deaths as a result of abuse. In Nova Scotia, the number of reported cases doubled in 1984 over the previous year. Authorities in Saint John, New Brunswick claim sexual offences against children and young people are among the fastest growing crimes. In Saskatchewan, there was a 300 per cent increase in the number of reported cases of abuse between 1979 and 1984. This figure also includes a dozen abused-relat-ed deaths. All across Canada abuse statistics are jumping. Sexual assault homicides are also on the increase in both real and proportional terms. These figures have more than doubled between the early 1960s and the late 1970s.
My Bill can be divided into two parts. The first part introduces new provisions regarding sexual abuse to a person under the age of 16 years. The second part lengthens the terms of punishment for assaults inflicted upon persons under the age of 16 years.
I should like to take this opportunity to deal in depth with the fundamental provisions of the Bill, but time does not allow me to do so. In conclusion, let me indicate that immense frustrations are felt by people all across the country. There is a concern that most cases of child abuse go unreported. Efforts must be made quickly to protect children in conjunction with efforts to make the public more aware. They must complement the efforts of our social agencies and our law enforcers. It is my hope that the Bill will bolster and contribute to the deterrent aspect of the law. Deterrence is a part of our justice system and is a major factor in the arrest of this crime. If awareness is created because of the Bill, it will be a positive step forward. My position is simply that if the Bill or awareness of the material contained in it, which will hopefully be referred to committee, should save one child from abuse, the substance of the Bill and my efforts will have had some purpose.

We should address the issue of the age of consent. If the age of consent remains at 14 years, as it is in the current Criminal Code, that is one
Criminal Code
particular point of view. If the age of consent is raised to 16 years, that is another particular point of view. We cannot bring in a Bill which changes the age of consent to 16 years except when two 15 year old teenagers are involved in a relationship. Essentially that is the effect of that particular provision. I think there is some confusion and inconsistency which will be dealt with in the reference to committee.
In trying to develop laws which we perceive as flexible, sometimes we create labyrinths that would be an absolute horror show for the courts to pursue and, in fact, would be in violation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Now is the time for the Government to bring forward some specific changes to the Criminal Code. I would hope that the reference to committee of this Private Member's Bill would precipitate the receipt of some answers from the Government rather than another study to look into the private sector's response to the Badgley Report.
Certainly, the Hon. Member who presented the Bill has the will to get to the root of the problem with the legislation. However, I would further point out that all of us, in our daily lives, have to reach beyond the simple issue of changing laws. Again, the Hon. Member for Outremont has said:

Obviously, the answer to family violence does not reside simply in a new definition of existing criminal offences, but in a change of attitudes as concerns enforcement of the law.
This means, Mr. Speaker, that if the rules are changed to say that someone will be sent to prison for 10, 14 or 15 years.

Criminal Code
this will not change public attitudes to this problem because, as mentioned by the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) most of the incidents and cases of abuse occur within the family or among people who know these children and who will never be reported to the authorities.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING CHILD ABUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak on behalf of the New Democratic Party on this private Member's Bill dealing with child sexual abuse. I would like to commend the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) for bringing this important subject and on the whole very reasonable proposals for changes in the law to the House for discussion. I will certainly support the reference of the Bill to committee for further study.
In reading the recommendations, the survey results and the vast amount of research that came from the Badgley Report, most people were struck by the extent of the problem of child sexual abuse. We all know that it exists, but I do not think the people understand just how pervasive it is. One-half of Canadian women and one-third of Canadian men have at some time been victims of a sexual offence. In the great majority of cases, 80 per cent of the time, these offences have occurred during childhood. It is children who are particularly vulnerable, and an increasisng number of them are very young children.
This is not to say that the problem itself is increasing. Badgley warned against being alarmist about this. The problem has existed for many, many years. It is not getting worse, but it has always been bad and very vigorous measures are needed to deal with it.
Of the victims, three-quarters of the women and nine-tenths of the men did not seek any assistance or make a report after the event in question. Many of the offences committed did not cause physical harm, but the psychological harm caused has been enormous. People suffer for years and years after the fact with psychological problems, emotional problems, problems in marriage and problems with relationships. Child sexual abuse often results in alcohol and drug abuse among victims.
Some of these offences are themselves physically serious, although these are a minority. Four per cent of girls were raped and a similar number of boys were homosexually raped. Twenty per cent of females were victims of exposure and 9 per cent of boys were victims of exposure. Some people may think that that is always a harmless offence, but the Badgley Report tells us otherwise. It tells us that it is a myth that exposure may be an unpleasant event but is not something to worry about. Eight per cent of the females and 4 per cent of the boys who were victims of sexual exposure were also sexually assaulted. In spite of the great seriousness of these offences and the importance of the Badgley Report, in the time the
February 13, 1986

Government has had we have not seen the action which we should have seen. I would point out to Hon. Members that the Government has had a year and a half since Badgley reported in the summer of 1984. 1 would now like to quote from the conclusions of the report which state:
Sexual offences are committed so frequently and against so many persons that there is an evident and urgent need to afford victims greater protection than that now being provided. The findings of the National Population Survey clearly show the compelling nature of the fears and stigma associated with having been a victim of a sexual offence.
Badgley continues:
What is required is the recognition by all Canadians that children and youths have the absolute right to be protected from these offences. To achieve this purpose, a major shift in the fundamental values of Canadians and in social policies by Government must be realized.
The report adds that if no action is taken, or if only token action is taken, then the risk is intolerably high that sexual abuse will continue.
Among the recommendations in the Badgley Report, the first two are of particular importance. They have been singled out throughout the report for comment. The first proposal was that owing to the complexity of the problem because of the number of agencies, the levels of government, the different professions, the medical people and police who deal with victims of sexual abuse, there be an office of commissioner for the implementation of these recommendations. This commissioner would report to the Prime Minister, would be responsible for legal and social reform and co-ordinate the work with voluntary agencies and other government Departments. The second proposal is that there be extensive public education and health promotion on the issue for prevention purposes.
I stress these two very positive recommendations of the report which Badgley recommends become law. Of course, the proposals we have before us today are with respect to changes in penalty. That is one way in which a society can say: "We disapprove of this. We do not want you to do it and we will punish you if you do". So society can make its views very clear.
Education is also extremely important, as are all types of support services. I regret to say that the Government has been very negligent in not acting on these matters. Unfortunately, the Hon. Member is not in a position with a Private Member's Bill to spend any money, nor is he in a position to advocate further reforms. What is needed is vigorous Government attention to the problem.
I would now like to deal with some of the specifics in the Bill. First, I would like to deal with Section 146(1) regarding the position of authority offence. This is interesting new concept. It breaks new ground in terms of our legal provisions. It is similar to the recommendation Badgley makes but it is not exactly the same. The wording is not as specific as that of Badgley who warned against the continued use of vague language. The position of authority offence is an important one because so much of sexual abuse is committed by people in positions of authority, whether it be authority by age, author-
Criminal Code
ity because one is a parent or some other adult in the family, or because someone is known to a child and is in a position of authority. This makes children particularly vulnerable. The stigma is great, as is the aftermath, because the victim has to continue to interact with the aggressor in the situation.
Section 158(1) would give protection to the victim. This is similar to those provisions which forbid the evidence of a victim of a sexual assault, generally, having had previous sexual activity with another person brought into court except under particular circumstances. My concern here is that the wording is not strong enough to protect victims of sexual assault. We have a long history of victims who have been placed on trial and their past history has been brought up and related at great length to the courts. Thus, the victim becomes the person being scrutinized.
Section 140 deals with the age of consent. The Bill would have the age raised to 16. There is also a proviso with respect to a three-year age difference. This is, of course, a contentious matter which could clearly have enforcement problems, especially with the three-year difference. Badgley recommends an increase in the age of consent to 16 but does not recommend the three-year difference. The reason for raising the age of consent to 16, even in a time when sexual mores are changing, is because of health considerations, quite apart from any moral ones, which are sometimes debatable in that some people share them and some do not. However, the health requirements apply to everyone. The dangers of pregnancy are much greater for girls under 16, as are complications in cases of abortion for young women who are pregnant.
Section 146 deals with physical contact for the purposes of sexual gratification or sexual stimulation. It provides for different levels of penalty depending upon the age of the victim. This provision is a gender-free provision. I would like to note that the gender-free world in criminal law can be rather foolish and sometimes go too far. We certainly want equality of opportunity. We want men and women, boys and girls, to be free and equal members of society. However, there are physical differences between the sexes. I am disturbed by some of the criminal cases we have seen in which judges have said: "This is discrimination in the law because it is an offence for a sexual act against a girl under 14 but not for a boy under 14". The judges have said that this is discrimination against men who commit these offences against girls. It is absolutely preposterous. Boys under the age of 14-boys at any age-do not get pregnant. There is a physical difference which requires that there be particular protection for girls. One hopes that the legalists will not be so caught up in the concept of equality and that they will treat this as a challenge, a vision, and not miss the important fact of life that protection is really needed for young girls.
Finally, I would like to deal with Section 245. This is a section which specifies a higher penalty for sexual assault of child victims as compared to older victims. This is the area in which I had the most reservations because sexual assault is reprehensible no matter what age the victim is. 1 think we would probably find some sexual assaults more repugnant than

February 13, 1986
Criminal Code
others, especially in the case of very young children, disabled persons who are unable to defend themselves or, similarly, very elderly people who are unable to defend themselves. Otherwise, I do not see why age should be a factor. Sexual assault is repugnant in any circumstances. I have reservations about making differences in penalties.
I would like to make a final comment on the issue of penalties. They are high in the Badgley Report and in this Private Member's Bill. We must realize that raising penalties for offences will not necessarily give people any greater protection. We know that people receive greater protection from the probability of being detected and dealt with as an offender. That seems to have more effect than the length of the penalty. Raising the penalties should not give us a false sense of security. It should not make us think that this will somehow give people protection. I do not think that differences of this sort will have any kind of impact. We know that if 10-year imprisonment penalties were brought in for parking offences, then people's parking offences would certainly go down since that type of difference would make people change their ways. However, an offence with an already heavy penalty will not be much more of a detriment if two or three years is added to the penalty. People do not read the laws and check to see whether penalties are 12, 14 or 15 years and gear their behaviour accordingly. People do not make decisions in that way.
If we want to give protection to children, which I am sure all Members would want to do, what we have to do is provide education, prevention and work with the provinces and the voluntary agencies to do all of those things in order to provide a really safe environment for the children of Canada.
