subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-LAKE ONTARIO-UNITED STATES PROGRAM TO CLEAN UP CHEMICAL DUMP
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-LAKE ONTARIO-UNITED STATES PROGRAM TO CLEAN UP CHEMICAL DUMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you are aware, some 20 per cent of all Canadians draw their drinking water either from the Niagara River or from water that has passed through the Niagara River. Along the shores of the Niagara River on the American side there are many toxic chemical dumps, but four in particular stand out in my mind, and I suspect the minds of most people who are familiar with that problem. Those dumps are the Love Canal site, the Hyde Park dump, the S Area dump and the 102nd Street dump.
All of these create a great potential danger for Canadians and Americans who draw their drinking water from the
Adjournment Debate
Niagara River, Lake Ontario and down the St. Lawrence River to the Atlantic Ocean. I have described those dumps as four obscenities on the American side of the Niagara River. I also think of them as a gigantic catastrophe that is waiting to happen.
In November last year, the United States Government, the Government of the State of New York and the owners of the Hyde Park dump, Occidental Chemical Company, came to an agreement relating to the clean-up of that particular dump with a view to ensuring that there would not be the potential of seepage of these toxic chemicals into the Niagara River and Lake Ontario.
Shortly thereafter, on November 28, I addressed a question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Gurbin) about that agreement. He indicated to me at that time that first, the agreement provided for the clean-up of certain chemicals in those dumps and for the containment and destruction of certain of those chemicals. However, we are all aware that there are a great many chemicals in that dump, at least 25 toxic chemicals. We are concerned whether all of those toxic chemicals or just a portion of them are being cleaned up.
The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary indicated at that time that the position of our Government, as we all hope and desire, is that the agreement is not just to contain the chemicals but to remove and destroy them. He also indicated that the Minister and the Department of the Environment in Canada were assessing the whole agreement to see whether or not it solved the problem of the Hyde Park dump as far as we in this country were concerned. He also indicated that there were 60 days after the agreement had been reached before the American Courts had the opportunity to approve or disapprove that agreement. That period of time has obviously passed since November 28, so I hope the Parliamentary Secretary is going to shed some light on this situation.
First, will he tell us whether or not that agreement was satisfactory to Canada, whether it will contain not just the toxic chemicals but also provide a mechanism for destroying them. I hope he will also tell us the details, if any, of the approval by the U.S. Courts on this subject.
Since I asked that question, there have been other developments. The head of the Environmental Protection Agency indicated his concern that the Super Fund which the American Congress set up to clean up chemical dump sites across the U.S. is in danger of running out of money. He indicated the money will probably run out in April of this year, and no more funding will be available. There are, of course, three proposals for providing more funds. There is a proposal before the U.S. House of Representatives which would provide some $10 billion by way of a tax on the petrochemical industry. There is a proposal before the U.S. Senate for a fund of some $7.5 billion financed by a manufacturing tax. There is a proposal by President Reagan for a fund of $5.8 billion to be funded by a petrochemical tax as well.

February 13, 1986
Adjournment Debate
When I was in Washington in September of 1985, this matter was up in the air and there has not been agreement since then. We are now six months along the road and if there is no agreement now or in April of this year, the Super Fund money will disappear. That includes the funding to clean up some 2,000 dump sites in the U.S., 105 of which are around the Great Lakes. I hope the funding to be provided by this agreement we are talking about for Hyde Park is not dependent on the Super Fund. If it is, we are going to face another potential setback, or even disaster, before we can get the Hyde Park site cleaned up.
That site, of course, is only one of the potential problems along the Niagara frontier. The other three I referred to are just as dangerous. I hope we will hear from the Parliamentary Secretary tonight some words of wisdom, encouragement and hope, indeed, definitive words concerning a clean-up, first of all of the Hyde Park dump site, a clean-up of the Love Canal dump site, the S Area dump site, as well as the 102 Street dump. If we are going to have safe water for about four million Canadians who draw their water from the Niagara River and the Great Lakes, we have to get those dumps cleaned up, and fast.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-LAKE ONTARIO-UNITED STATES PROGRAM TO CLEAN UP CHEMICAL DUMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I doubt any Member of Parliament could have made the point more forcefully or clearly than the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). I will try and deal with the specific points he has raised.
February 24 is not 60 days from November 28. It happens to be the end of the 60-day period which the U.S. Court defined for public comment on the proposal. I regret to have to inform the Hon. Member that our position and the final determination of the U.S. Court is keyed to February 24. I cannot offer him any more specific comment than I did on the day he asked me the question.
The second point, to amplify and precisely explain what the Hon. Member said concerning the danger which exists in the four areas referred to, in fact in the Hyde Park area alone there is probably a ton of dioxin. As the Hon. Member has mentioned, this is one of four specific areas, but there are many other point sources that have been identified along the American border as well as the Canadian border. On balance, probably about 90 per cent is coming from the American side. However, we both take water, and that area serves between four million and six million people for drinking water supplies. It then runs down through Lake Ontario and out into the St. Lawrence River. The Member has very clearly identified the situation in the United States.
The dependency of the super funding for this, as far as I know, is not really an issue for this specific resolution. This is a court determination of a settlement with a chemical company that has a responsibility. This is really what is being worked through now. The EPA is very much involved, as are the American courts. My understanding is that the total job is very much dependent on the Super Fund. One of the Bills
which the Member mentioned has passed one of the Houses. We do not know where they will all end up.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to make it very clear that we are talking about a very complex and untried type of situation in terms of the technologies and the clean-up that needs to be done. I will correct any impression that was left that we are only interested in some of the chemicals. The final position of the Canadian Government is that none of the chemicals which exist in that dump site or other dump sites can be allowed to escape through the dump sites and into the Niagara River. That is our final position and that is what we must aim for.
The question is how we are going to reach that goal and how effective is the initial stage of the solution that is being discussed. What is being discussed is a containment proposal which, along with the containment, removes chemicals that would have otherwise seeped through which will, in turn, be destroyed.
The technologies that are important here have to do with the problems that will exist in dump sites in both the United States and Canada in terms of massive volumes of contaminated soil that would have to be transported if we were talking about excavation and removal. We must develop technologies that will extract the chemicals from those sites so that we can avoid other serious dangers involved in transportation. We would still end up having to eventually destroy those chemicals. It is a continuum, Mr. Speaker. Our position is final. We do not want any more of these toxic chemicals in the Niagara River.

subtopic: JUSTICE-ENQUIRY WHY ANGLOPHONE APPOINTED INSTEAD OF AVAILABLE FRANCOPHONE

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: JUSTICE-ENQUIRY WHY ANGLOPHONE APPOINTED INSTEAD OF AVAILABLE FRANCOPHONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 4, 1985, we asked the Minister of Justice why he failed to appoint six bilingual francophones to the Court of Appeal of Ontario, in view of the great number of Frenchspeaking lawyers and judges available. That question, Mr. Speaker, was in no way aimed at disparaging a judge who is known for his qualifications and credibility. It was simply aimed at understanding the behaviour of a Government that ignored the dearly acquired rights of 500,000 Frenchspeaking Ontarians. In any event, Mr. Speaker, the Minister answered that the important thing was to appoint a first-class person, in other words there was no first class person among our Francophone jurists.
Mr. Speaker, since 1953, the tradition in Ontario was that at least one bilingual French-speaking judge should be appointed to the Ontario Court of Appeal. Although this gave no additional rights to the Francophones, French-speaking Ontarians were proud of having such a representative, until their rights would finally be recognized.
It was therefore in May 1984 that the Ontario Government finally passed the Courts of Justice Act, 1984. As we know,
February 13, 1986

that Act allowed the 500,000 French-speaking Ontarians to be heard by a judge or judges speaking their own language. For French-speaking Canadians, that new Act was a giant stride along the road to rights they had always been denied.
The Mulroney Government comes to power and with it a 33-year old tradition disappears. In fact, by appointing Justice Horace Krever to the Ontario Court of Appeal, the Minister of Justice of the Conservative Government has broken with this tradition and, I feel, violated the right of Franco-Ontarians to have a sufficient number of permanent Francophone judges to hear their cases in their own language.
Mr. Speaker, the next day, on February 5, in reply to another question, the Minister answered: There are 18 judges at the appeal level in Ontario, three of whom are bilingual, or 17 per cent. There are an additional four bilingual judges who can be used on appeals from the High Court. Of these seven, four are Francophones. In 1985 there were two appeals among 1,400 applications which required a French panel. What the Minister omitted to say was that of those 18 judges, 16 are permanent and two are supernumerary. Of the 16 permanent judges, only two are bilingual, while three judges are needed to hear a case, to form the minimum quorum of three judges at the Court of Appeal-what is referred to as a panel. The Minister therefore admitted that he felt like using a supernumerary judge or the bilingual judges from the Superior Court to constitute the so-called panel.
Mr. Speaker, this is absurd, especially since the problem could easily have been avoided by appointing a bilingual Francophone judge to the Court of Appeal! Furthermore, when he stated that only two appeals had been heard in 1985, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) forgot that the 1984 Courts of Justice Act is not in effect throughout Ontario, but will be by the end of July. By his comments, the Minister also quantified the rights of Canadian Francophones. He, of all people, should know that one does not quantify a right and that rights are given freely and generously to all.
Mr. Speaker, on February 5 last week, I also asked the Prime Minister what he thought of this appointment and whether he agreed with his Minister of Justice that no bilingual Francophone could be found for this position. I was frustrated if not shocked at the Prime Minister's reply. He claimed he had personally contacted a Francophone judge or lawyer-he was not sure-he said he was distinguished and that for health reasons he had been unable to accept the appointment. He had to decline, according to the Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, these comments do not make sense, to say the least, when we know that in the Province of Ontario we have at least fifteen very good lawyers and fifteen judges in the courts at the present time who could easily fill the position of
Adjournment Debate
Judge of the Court of Appeal and would make very competent and, incidentally, very healthy legal experts.
The Court of Appeal of the Province of Quebec has a total of 15 bilingual permanent judges, four of whom are Anglophones, while the 1984 legislation on judicial courts in Ontario gives Francophones the right to be heard in their own language by a judge who speaks that language. Why do we not have at least one judge-one is not very much to ask for-one permanent bilingual French-speaking judge to the Court of Appeal? Is that not a blatant injustice to French-speaking Ontarians?
Mr. Speaker, in an interview with the media, the Minister of Justice claimed that all the fuss about the appointment of a French-speaking judge to the Court of Appeal is nothing but a charade to discredit him for being unilingual. That statement goes to prove that actually the Minister does not understand anything about Francophones. He does not understand anything about the daily reality of 500,000 French-speaking Ontarians. Francophones are not concerned about the Minister of Justice being unilingual. What francophones care about is the rights they are being deprived of by the Minister of Justice. This is not a political issue but a matter of justice and equity, supported by the non-political, and I repeat non-political association of the French-speaking legal profession in Ontario, by the once again non-political Commissioner of Official languages of Canada, and also by one of his own colleagues, the Hon. Member for Richelieu (Mr. Plamondon).
Mr. Speaker, for all those reasons, it is clear the Minister of Justice does not care about French-speaking Canadians. By gulping his words, the Prime Minsiter has shown that Francophones cannot depend on this Conservatives Government to safeguard their rights. This could not be more tragic, when we think of the numerous efforts of the French-speaking community in Ontario to acquire those rights.
By appointing a unilingual English-speaking judge to a seat that was traditionally reserved to a bilingual French-speaking judge, the Minister has broken a 33-year tradition. It is sad that this Government's vision, in the context of a bilingual country, is very much different from the approach and views of that government.
Mr. Speaker, I would conclude by saying that we do not ask for much, we are only asking for justice, we are asking that one of the members of the Court of Appeal of Ontario be a bilingual francophone.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Valcourt (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: JUSTICE-ENQUIRY WHY ANGLOPHONE APPOINTED INSTEAD OF AVAILABLE FRANCOPHONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is amazing that the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), whom I was told had a reputation for being a defender of the rights of French-speaking minorities not only in Ontario but all across Canada, to see him use the appointment of Mr. Justice Krever to score political points on the back of the Government, tell all Canadians that the Conservative Government does not care about francophones outside Quebec, and suggest that only the

February 1 3, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Liberal Party cares about them. As Parliamentary Secretary and also as a French-speaking Member of Parliament from outside Quebec and an Acadian from New Brunswick, I can assure the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) that, as long as the Government Members will remain alert, which they have always been, as I can see every day, Canadians have nothing to fear.
When someone rises as the Hon. Member has just done to embarrass someone who has been appointed to the Court of Appeal, in this case, Mr. Justice Krever, whose ability the Hon. Member is not questioning as he speaks only of tradition, he should also look at what services are available to Franco-Ontarians. Everyone is entitled to be heard in French by Ontario courts, French-speaking magistrates are always available. Seven members of the Ontario Supreme Court are perfectly bilingual and four of them are francophones.
The appointment of Mr. Justice Krever is the result of consultations with the Chief Justice of Ontario and the Attorney General of Ontario, Mr. Ian Scott, who has even supported publicly the appointment of Mr. Justice Krever and confirmed that he was consulted from the very beginning about the whole procedure. The Ontario Attorney General even added, Mr. Speaker, that he did not understand why the federal Liberal Party was raising this issue and using it to try and suggest that we do not care about francophones outside Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, when someone speaks about an obvious injustice, we have to look at what is in fact happening. The information at the Department of Justice is that Franco-Ontarians can be served properly in their own language by the Court of Appeal and the Ontario Superior Court, and the appointment of Mr. Justice Krever was approved by chief justices throughout Canada, including the Chief Justice of the Quebec Superior Court. This attack on the character of Mr. Justice Krever is sure to be embarrassing for a man who has devoted so many years to the service of justice. He was appointed because of his ability and because he was the best choice.
Finally, I can assure you that the rights of all francophones in Canada are a priority consideration for the Minister of Justice, whatever the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier might suggest, and that all francophones can be heard in their own language in Ontario.

subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-PORTRAYAL OF WOMEN IN THE MEDIA. (B) APPOINTMENTS TO CRTC AND CBC
STATUS OF WOMEN-PORTRAYAL OF WOMEN IN THE MEDIA. (B) APPOINTMENTS TO CRTC AND CBC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 3, I raised a very important question with the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) regarding the report on industry self-regulation entitled "Sex Role Stereotyping in the Broadcast Media". The report shows that effectively there has been no progress made in improving the portrayal
of women and participation of women in the broadcast media. The Minister did not care to comment upon the report, although previous reports have also shown no progress. They have been available for many months, particularly the "Media Watch" report and the report by the CBC itself.
The Minister gave his assurance that decisions of the Government would be based upon discussions held in hearings which are to be scheduled in three Canadian cities. 1 have to ask: Why three more hearings? The question has been studied far too long without action. The problems have been documented for years. I asked him another question about action the Government could take immediately and had entirely at its disposal, and that is with the appointments to the CRTC and the CBC, which should be half and half, men and women, according to our notion of equality of the sexes.
The Minister gave a very poor reply here as well. He mentioned the name of one woman whom he had appointed. Well, there are seven men and five women on the CBC board, and there are three vacancies. There is certainly an opportunity to have equal representation. I hope that among the next appointments there will be people who know something about the subject of the failure to give adequate portrayal of women and who will use that opportunity to put pressure on the CBC. This is one thing Government can do in its appointments. It cannot interfere in the operations of the CBC. That would be entirely improper. However, it could appoint people who will say that equality for women demands fair treatment in the broadcast media.
With regard to the CRTC, there is also an underrepresentation of women. There are currently 14 men and seven women appointed. Canada, in making recommendations to the United Nations for the plan of action, recommended in its communication section that half the appointments be of women to Government appointed boards in that field. It is quite wrong that the Government has not acted here. It is hypocritical when we consider that this was a Government of Canada recommendation to the United Nations.
What are the facts? In the two years of so-called self-regulation, which industry asked for, they said: "We don't want Government regulation, don't touch the Broadcasting Act, don't make us do anything. We will reform on our own and in two years we will show you what a wonderful job we have done". It has done almost nothing, and some statistics show a deterioration of the situation.
Let me begin with CBC English channels. I will start with one statistic in the area of drama; how men and women are shown at the place of work. Who is the supervisor and who is the employee reporting to a supervisor? In 1981, 71 per cent were male supervisors, 26 per cent female. In 1983, the number of men had increased so it was 81 per cent male and 16 per cent female. On The National, the major newscast of the country, in 1981 there were 8 per cent women reporters. It rose to a grand total of 18 per cent, one of the few statistics to show any increase. That is only to 18 per cent. Of the
February 13, 1986

interviewees, 16 per cent were female 1981 and only 13 per cent in 1983, a deterioration. The anchor people were all men and all the substitutes were men.
On the expert witnesses, we do not get information year by year, but the average is 5 per cent. It is certainly an insulting notion that 5 per cent of the expertise in Canada is female and the other 95 per cent is male, that somehow women are not as capable as men.
Even for random interviewees, only 36 per cent were female. Women, who only have to be alive and have a comment to make, are underrepresented. For the French network, in drama the situation in 1981 was 77 per cent male, up to 78 per cent in 1982. Women were badly underrepresented. [Translation]
On the French network in 1980-1981, announcers on newscasts and other current events programs were men and women, respectively 57 per cent and 43 per cent. In 1981, 1982 and 1984, 82 per cent were men and 18 per cent were women, therefore a drop in the representation of women. In 1980, 29 per cent of interviewees were women, but that figure dropped as low as 15 per cent in 1984.
The percentage of women reporters in 1980 was 20 per cent, dropping to 12 per cent in 1984.

These are appalling statistics. For children, the cartoon characters are 61 per cent male and 16 per cent female. Even the portrayal of who is alive and doing things in cartoons for children overrepresents men. To add to those statistics, 23 per cent of neither sex. Therefore, women are very, very badly underrepresented. Voice-overs in English advertising, 91 per cent had a voice-over, of these 90 per cent were men and only 6 per cent women and four of both sexes.

And the same thing goes for French advertising.

Women are twice as likely as men to be shown partially clothed. Women are shown as sex objects on television. As far as age distribution goes, there are fewer women and younger women as well. The study showed very few trends because it was an expensive study and it would be very hard to replicate. We are concerned that the CRTC has not provided the material in a way that it can be replicated so that progress reports can be made.
There have been vigorous recommendations for action. I would hope that the Government would begin to act on this serious question. If women are to be equal in Canadian society, they must have equal access to the airwaves. Women's events must be covered equally with those of men and women must be seen as experts and as full participants in Canadian society. There are many recommendations from Media Watch and other women's organizations as to practical measures the Government could be taking to that end.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-PORTRAYAL OF WOMEN IN THE MEDIA. (B) APPOINTMENTS TO CRTC AND CBC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has raised an important issue and we are all, I am sure, appreciative of her concerns about the problem of sex-role stereotyping in the broadcast media. I would like to provide some background information on this issue to the House.
In September 1979, at the request of the Government, the CRTC established a task force on sex-role stereotyping. In September 1982, the task force released its report entitled "Images of Women" which called for industry self-regulation with public accountability to improve the portrayal of women in the programming and commercial content broadcast by the Canadian broadcasting system. This report was the culmination of three years of co-operative effort among members of the broadcasting and advertising industries, the public and the CRTC.
As recommended by the task force, a two-year period of industry self-regulation, beginning September 1, 1982, was undertaken. The CRTC has recently released a report summarizing the initiatives taken during this self-regulatory period as well as the results of an independent content analysis of Canadian broadcast programming conducted at the request of the CRTC.

The Hon. Member asked the Minister of Communications what was the Government's position with respect to the report on the self-regulation period which has just ended. I would like to repeat the remarks made by the Minister in the House, and more particularly that it is too early for the Government to make any comment about it. The third phase of the process recommended by the CRTC task force is that the report be used as the basis for public discussions on the efficiency of industry self-regulation. With that in mind the CRTC has announced that public hearings on that subject will be held in April and May in Vancouver, in Montreal and in the National Capital Region. After these hearings the CRTC will assess the efficiency of self-regulation and decide whether new measures might be considered.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member also asked the Minister of Communication about the Government's intention concerning the appointment of women to the CRTC and the CBC board of directors. The Minister clearly indicated that increased woman representation and participation in these areas was a major consideration and that he would keep that in mind when vacancies occurred. In this connection, the Minister mentioned the recent appointment of Mrs. Lorraine Duguay as Director of the CBC. I am sure that the House shares the Minister's eagerness to appoint competent women such as Mrs. Duguay to important positions.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make clear to the House that the Government recognizes that the problem of sex-role stereotyping is a broad and complex one and one that

February 13, 1986
Adjournment Debate
will not disappear overnight. Indeed, as members of the CRTC task force have noted, societal attitudes toward women must change dramatically before that goal is entirely realizable. I would, however, like to reassure the House and the Hon. Member that the Government is following the CRTC's activities in this regard very carefully.
